#3455. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3454. Meet the Biggest Ralph Lauren Fan in France

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing company and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes

But how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a New York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

One might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”

If the self-made New Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

This story was originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3453. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Shocking Death Leaves Its Biggest Question Unanswered

In the land of Mordor, where the spoilers lie. This article covers major plot details from the Season 3 finale of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

How's that for a red herring? "The Rings of Power" Season 3 seemed to confirm one of the biggest fan-theories around: that Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), the sulky Southlander with an odd tendency to gravitate towards darkness, was well on his way to becoming one of the fearsome Nazgnagôl. The presumption among many has been that he wouldn't merely be a Ring Servant of Sauron (Charlie Vickers), in fact, but the greatest of them all, i.e. the Witch-king. The finale, however, decided to introduce a late contender for that dubious crown. Ever an agent of chaos, Sauron gifts one of his rings to the Dark Wizard Pallando (Ciarán Hinds) and even dubs him as "the greatest of the Nine — a Witch-king no man can slay." Case closed, right? Wrong!

Late in the episode, Pallando successfully turns away from the dark side (thanks to the good-natured urgings of Daniel Weyman's Gandalf, of course) and rejects all the seductive offers that come with Sauron's ring ... but sacrifices his life to save his "old friend." This shocking death resolves one storyline while adding all sorts of question marks to another. As Gandalf makes his way westward with merry ol' Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear), that appears to close the book on the action in Rhûn. At the same time, however, we're still left wondering about where, exactly, Theo fits into all this mess. Is he merely meant to be one of the lower-ranked members of the Ringwraiths, doomed to forever take orders (and abuse) from his Dark Lord? Or is he still a Witch-king in the making?

Did anyone expect Pallando's arc to end quite like this? The former Blue Wizard who murdered his own friend Alatar may not have seemed like the most obvious candidate for redemption, but Gandalf manages to pull him back from the brink just in time to help save the day and lessen Sauron's forces significantly. Unfortunately, he succumbs to his wound inflicted by the Nazgnagôl known as Khamûl (Zubin Varla) and passes away dramatically — complete with the stunning visual of his spirit actually departing his body and making its way west, well beyond the sight of mere mortals. Despite seemingly paralleling the storyline of the white wizard Saruman's downfall (played by Christopher Lee in Peter Jackson's Middle-earth films), Pallando rewrites his own ending.

It puts a fitting and satisfying enough bow on a subplot that had finally run out of juice. It's just not that the empty wastelands of Rhûn are visually boring, the action far too removed from the rest of Middle-earth to feel all that urgent (no matter how many hundreds of thousands of enemies live there), and the tone just a little too close to "Harry Potter" for our liking. It's all of that, plus the fact that this prolonged showdown with Pallando prevented Gandalf from ever interacting with the rest of our main heroes. It's long past time for our favorite wizard to cross paths with the likes of Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo), and Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker) and finally feel like an integral member of this story, and now, he's finally free to do so.

Either way, RIP Pallando, the most gloriously bearded wizard in all of Middle-earth (and with an attitude to match).

Speaking of subplots without much juice, well, there's no nice way to say this: Theo, we are officially done with your nonsense. Barely one episode after coming oh-so-close to rejecting Sauron's offer and proving that the Men of Middle-earth still have some genuine fight left in them, our unconvincing antagonist begins the finale right back by Sauron's side after failing to destroy his ring. Still, even that wouldn't be so bad if we at least received some clarity regarding this whole Witch-king business. With Pallando out of the picture and Khamûl seemingly dead (although, in fairness, we never see his body after he's thrown out of Sauron's tower of Barad-dûr), well, Theo's pretty much the leading contender by default, no?

Well, it's more complicated than that. Theo's first real interaction with Sauron in the finale is as the deliverer of bad news, informing his Dark Lord that half their army has deserted following Pallando's death and (presumably) the breaking of the spell he had cast upon them. And, as you can imagine, this doesn't exactly go well for him as Sauron grabs him by the throat and demands to know why he couldn't stop them.

But perhaps their last scene together holds some clues. While preparing for battle with the combined force of Númenor and the Elves, Sauron slips off his One Ring and gives himself up to his enemies. It's unlikely he'd keep carrying that on his person, so did he perhaps entrust his most "precious" creation to Theo? Is this all part of an evil plan that will see the Southlander ascend to the ultimate position of authority among the Ringwraiths? We'll sadly have to wait for Season 4.

After more than a decade of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. But there's one group of players who aren't so thrilled about the level of realism in GTA 6: snake owners.

Over on Reddit, a post from the r/mildlyinfuriating subreddit about GTA 6 has garnered more than 92,000 likes in just a few days. The user was eager to share the game with a friend from southern Florida. However, rather than being dazzled by GTA 6's intricate attention to detail, the friend was horrified by Dolores the snake's habitat in Jason and Lucia's Key Lento bungalow.

The redditor wrote that their friend "went on this big long 10 minute rant about how the people that designed this game are idiots and terrible people and how they’re gonna cause people to go out and buy snakes and mistreat them and abandon them. Ultimately, the dismayed snake fan concluded, “They [Rockstar] spent 13 years on this thing and did no fucking research.” If you've actually spent any time at all with GTA 6, you'll realize this is a pretty wild exaggeration. #3450. Blade Runner 2099 Has A Subtle Reference To Ridley Scott's Alien Franchise

Ever since folks (including, presumably, Sir Ridley Scott) took a look at both "Alien" and "Blade Runner" and thought "Hmm, both of these films involve artificial humans...," the two franchises and their respective worlds have been latently linked. To be sure, the relationship between the pair has never reached the stage of things like "Alien vs. Predator" or "Predator: Badlands," in which the "Alien" and "Predator" franchises explicitly cross over. Yet, there have been clues to "Alien" and "Blade Runner" sharing a universe since the latter film was released.

In the original "Blade Runner," for example, Scott re-used a monitor graphic from "Alien" in one insert shot, causing folks to speculate on a potential shared universe. In the intervening years, Scott has subtly encouraged the connection as well. In fact, deep within the special features on the home media release of "Prometheus," an association was implied in an Easter egg audio log entry by the character of Peter Weyland (Guy Pearce), which obliquely refers to the Tyrell Corporation.

Now, though actual crossover has yet to take place, the relationship between the franchises continues apace with the release of this month's "Blade Runner 2099." It does so in a very clever, unexpected way, too, and not with the hiding of some other small Easter egg in the series' numerous environments and vehicles. (Which is not to say one doesn't exist, so keep hunting, hunters!)

Instead, the "Alien" reference in "Blade Runner 2099" is subtle even while being put right in your face. Literally, as it concerns the hood device which the Replicant Blade Runners use to subdue their human prey. This device seems like a gnarly, fascistic element on the surface, but its anatomy and deployment heavily recalls the facehugger from "Alien."

Although the signature scene from Ridley Scott's "Alien" is the chestburster sequence, the earlier attack by a facehugger leaping out of a Xenomorph egg has to be a close second. One could even argue that these moments, in tandem, represent the breakout moment of Ridley Scott's directing career. And while it's clear if it was showrunner Silka Luisa or someone else who decided to include a nod to the facehugger (like Scott, who's an executive producer on the series), the aforementioned "Blade Runner 2099" device is a devilishly clever callback that which fits perfectly within the show's world while doubling as a sly wink to Scott's past.

In "Blade Runner 2099," the Replicant uprising has already come and gone, leaving the remaining illegal (and/or resistant) humans on Earth at the mercy of Replicant Blade Runners. But where human Blade Runners typically "retired" illegal Replicants on sight, Replicant Blade Runners tend to capture humans alive first. To do so, they fit them with a hood device that makes the human unable to see or speak, the latter thanks to a tube instantly forced down their throat, slowly feeding them nutrients during their capture.

This, plus the way the Blade Runners violently slap on the hood and press the tube button, seems to deliberately recall how the facehugger operates. It's a great little touch that helps the series blur the lines of morality, making the Replicants simultaneously more humane than the human Blade Runners while being more violent and dehumanizing. So, in lieu of an eventual (?) proper "Blade Runner" and "Alien" crossover, for now, this is an effective way to ensure these two franchises continue to share so much thematic DNA.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now available to stream on Prime Video.

#3448. Jessica Chastain's 2026 Neo-Western Is A Surprise Streaming Hit On Netflix

"Heartland" is written and directed by Shana Feste, whose last project was the Prime Video supernatural horror film "Run Sweetheart Run." Prior to that, Feste made her directorial debut with 2009's "The Greatest" before helming the 2010 music drama "Country Strong." That one starred Gwynyth Paltrow as a recovering alcoholic country singer, and with "Heartland," Feste once again gives us a hard drinkin' songstress with a self-destructive streak. This time, however, she's out for justice.

Chastain's Misty Jones, as it were, is a former country music legend who's led a secluded life in Georgia ever since leaving her singing career behind. But when her niece Charlie Heart (Carter Faith) disappears, the so-called "Queen of Mean" returns to Nashville, Tennessee, to uncover the truth about what happened. But as she embarks on her quest, she uncovers a side of the city she's never seen and is forced to confront her past. Sounds alright, doesn't it? Well, Netflixers are absolutely loving Chastain's quest for justice.

"Heartland" is a strange mix of mystery thriller and noir scored by a country soundtrack that features original music from Carter Faith, who also happens to be a real-life country music star. Shana Feste appears to have taken some cues from a number of Taylor Sheridan shows in that regard, which has proven out to have been a wise move — at least, if the Netflix viewing figures are anything to go by.

"Heartland" hit Netflix on November 13, 2026, and became an instant hit. The film debuted at the top of the English movie list with 7.3 million views, finishing its first week at number two on the global movies charts with 14.8 million views. Since then it's been smooth sailing for "Heartland," according to FlixPatrol.

In point of fact, the film has remained in the top 10 in the United States for the last 10 days, hovering around the number one and two spots before dropping to number five on November 22, 2026, and number six as of November 24. But that's just part of the story, as "Heartland" is also a global hit. The film was a top 10 movie in 89 countries during the week of November 11 to November 22, 2026, and is still charting in 78 countries at the time of writing. It even hit number one in Australia and New Zealand in its second week on Netflix. All in all, then, that's a pretty good showing for "Heartland," which otherwise received mixed reviews from critics.

Writer/director Shana Feste told Texas Monthly that her aim with "Heartland" was to subvert established norms of the thriller, crime, and action genres. "We have this very established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men," she noted. "But we are not so generous with our female characters." Feste went on to describe the experience of creating Misty Jones as "incredibly freeing," due to the fact this was a character "that did not organize her life around being liked or desired." That certainly makes for a compelling protagonist in the film, and Jessica Chastain does a solid job of rendering the "Queen of Mean" in all her damaged glory.

Sadly, that only amounted to a less than impressive 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is five percentage points higher than the audience score. David Rooney of The Hollywood Reporter couldn't help himself when he described Feste's latest as "Country Weak," echoing the sentiments of The Guardian's Adrian Horton (who opined that "Heartland" "seems more destined for background music than a hit"). Nick Schager of The Daily Beast, on the other hand, thought the film managed to "offset its predictability with knockabout ferocity," and William Bibbiani of TheWrap liked it enough to hope it becomes "the first in a long, long series." With the viewership being what it is, that might just turn out to be the case.

"Heartland" might not be the best thriller Netflix has to offer, then. But it's not without its charms and comes with the Netflix audience seal of approval.

#3447. What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s new limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that company’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

“The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” says Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan says that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION

Not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

In episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

“One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”

As for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch plan: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the company’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF

True. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”

#3446. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Apple participates in Cyber Monday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy, Amazon, and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

It's hard not to think about these missing X-Men alums.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The highly anticipated Avengers: Doomsday not only promises sprawling action across the multiverse, but it also features a massive cast (as revealed by that chair promotion last year). However, while the film unites veterans of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and stars who predate it, there are some familiar faces who don’t appear to be in the fold. That includes X-Men veterans Halle Berry and Anna Paquin. I’ve been wondering why they weren’t invited back, and Joe and Anthony Russo shared their takes.

Doomsday features several beloved X-Men stars like Ian McKellen, James Marsden, Rebecca Romijn and the late, great Patrick Stewart (in his final film performance). So, for fans like myself, it’s a bit of a head-scratcher that Berry (who played Ororo Munroe/Storm) and Paquin (Marie D'Ancanto/Rogue) apparently weren’t invited to the party. As part of a cover story for this 2026 movie schedule entry, the Russo Brothers were asked about their absences and those of others, with Joe saying this:

[The casting] was really targeted. It was really specific.

In fairness, the Russos are shrewd when it comes to assembling (no pun intended) the ensembles for their MCU team-up films. Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame both had specific sets of characters that played into the films’ respective narratives in relevant ways. With that being said, considering the heavy presence of X-Men alums in Doomsday, it’s still somewhat weird that Storm, Rogue, Iceman and more aren’t present when Marsden’s Cyclops says, “To me, my X-Men.” Still, Anthony Russo added another point:

We really do have a process where we see the entire film through each character’s eyes, no matter what the size of their role is. With the X-Men, we got to really deep dive and think about their histories as characters, their experiences, and how this particular moment in time was gonna affect them. There’s such a rich history to them that we really do bring them to the film as if it’s their movie, as well.

Bringing those OGs into the fold seemed to be the realization of a dream not just for the Russos but for producer Kevin Feige as well. Feige’s producing career notably started years ago when Lauren Shuler Donner tapped him as an associate producer on 2000’s X-Men. Now, the super producer is in the position to have his MCU characters interact with the famous mutants for what may be the latter group’s final stand within the multiverse.

There’s still reason to wonder whether more characters are being kept under wraps ahead of the film’s release. However, earlier this year, when Berry was asked about possibly reprising Storm in Doomsday, she seemed to downplay the idea. The actress does still have plenty of love for the character and the franchise, though, as she celebrated X-Men’s 26th anniversary in July. That post also prompted fans to question her involvement in the upcoming Marvel movie, but nothing has seemingly materialized at this point.

What is known for sure, though, is that a new team of X-Men will be prominent within the MCU moving forward, as a reboot from director Jake Schreier is on the way. With that, new actors will be taking on the lead roles, with Inde Navarrette and Maya Boyd playing Rogue and Storm, respectively. There’s still time for Marvel to surprise us by having Halle Berry, Anna Paquin and others show up in Doomsday but, if not, there’s always Secret Wars.

Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on December 18, while Secret Wars is set to follow on December 17, 2027. In the meantime, grab a Disney+ subscription and stream the MCU and X-Men films.

#3444. Why Quentin Tarantino Didn't Direct Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth."

If it looks like a Quentin Tarantino movie and talks like a Quentin Tarantino movie, you'd usually find yourself watching a Quentin Tarantino movie. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is the rare exception to that rule, however. After "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" debuted in 2019 and was heralded by many as the filmmaker's best movie yet, whispers of a continuation soon grew to a deafening noise. Tarantino then went and wrote a book based on the events of the film in a sort of reverse-adaptation situation. He subsequently spent months talking up his intentions to direct a since-shelved project called "The Movie Critic," which would've starred Brad Pitt reprising his role as Cliff Booth. But after that fell apart, David Fincher eventually came on board to direct Tarantino's script for "Cliff Booth."

After having finally seen the highly-anticipated sequel for ourselves, we (and many others) were left with even more questions regarding why Tarantino ultimately decided to sit this one out rather than sit in the director's chair himself. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a solid enough spiritual successor, albeit one where Fincher and Tarantino's unique (and wildly different) sensibilities seem to clash more often than complement. And the snappiness of the dialogue, tone, and rhythm and pacing certainly feel indebted to the quintessential Tarantino style most of us know and adore.

So, with all due respect to a legend like Fincher, was there ever a world where Tarantino had simply directed this himself? It's a complicated question with no easy answers, but below, we've rounded up a complete timeline of events — to the best of public knowledge, of course. So, here's why Tarantino's "Cliff Booth" instead became a Fincher/Tarantino joint.

It all began, as it so often does in this business, with a project that wasn't to be. In 2023, "The Movie Critic" was breathlessly announced as Quentin Tarantino's 10th and final directing gig — a self-imposed limit that the ever-opinionated artist decided to stick to, no matter what. And while rumors initially suggested this might have been based on the life of prolific writer and critic Pauline Kael, it was later revealed that this would've been an original story taking QT's usual fast-and-loose approach to fact and fiction. All seemed ready and raring to go ... until Tarantino appeared to rethink his approach (following rewrites that delayed production) and dropped the project altogether.

But Hollywood just loves a comeback story, and this wasn't the end of the line. In 2025, news broke that Fincher would be directing a sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" focused on stuntman extraordinaire Cliff Booth. It didn't take much brain power to connect the dots between the two film ideas, leading to much informed speculation that Tarantino reworked his idea for "The Movie Critic" into what turned out to be "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." For his part, Tarantino spoke to The Hollywood Reporter in 2025 and denied that Cliff was ever going to appear in "The Movie Critic." Of course, this contradicts other accounts claiming that a sort of cinematic universe may have been in the works. We'll likely never know the full behind-the-scenes story.

Did we receive the next-best outcome in its place? A Fincher/QT dream team has been years in the making, after all. Still, we can't help but wonder about what might have been.

For better or worse, what's clear is that "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" seems fated to divide viewers. There are those who feel David Fincher's involvement as director meshes beautifully with Quentin Tarantino's skills as writer, leading to a final result that's even more than the sum of its mighty parts — akin to what Fincher pulled off in his collaboration with Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Network," for instance. But there are others who feel that, while the tension between their particular styles and worldviews makes for dramatically interesting material, the push and pull between Fincher and Tarantino ultimately proves too unwieldy.

Yes, I happen to fall into that latter camp (if you haven't guessed as much already), and it's tough to reconcile the movie we have with the hypothetical version it could've been. To be fair, the evidence is fairly plain to see. Where "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is overflowing with warmth and nostalgia and a poignant perspective of time passing us by (and, okay, a whole lot of gratuitous violence, too), "Cliff Booth" stands out for how emotionally distant and cold it feels in practically every scene ... outside of Cliff's flirtations with Elizabeth Debicki's Karen Crosby or bonding moments with father Gus (Peter Weller), at least.

In the hands of Tarantino alone, it's fair to wonder if he could've brought a much-needed sense of fun and verve to the action that seems oddly missing in "Cliff Booth." What we ended up with is something caught between a Fincher and Tarantino film. Instead of half of both, wouldn't it have been more satisfying to get all of Tarantino?

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in select theaters.

#3443. New 'GTA 6' Leak Is Great News For PC Gamers, But There's A Catch

A new leak gives PC players a sense of what to expect from GTA 6 with souped-up settings

Much has been said about the differences between Grand Theft Auto 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox, but how will Rockstar Games' open-world game fare on PC? An official port has yet to be announced, but a recent leak of the Xbox build of the game has kicked off a race to recompile the game and make it unofficially available on more platforms. As that work continues, yet another leak offers PC players some perspective on what might be possible in GTA 6 when the game isn't held down by console constraints.

On Wednesday, known GTA leaker Tex2 shared a Pastebin that lists GTA 6's apparent console settings shipped by Rockstar. These are tunable options that exist to help the game shine on platforms with varying capacities, like the less-powerful Xbox Series S. The text dump has since been pulled by Pastebin, but Polygon viewed the document before the platform made it unavailable.

Some aspects of the game, like Global Illumination Quality, Ray Traced Directional Shadows, and Texture Quality are already set to high on PlayStation 5. The same aspects are sometimes lower or altogether absent on Xbox, though reports suggest the platforms have more parity than Sony's marketing would like you to believe.

There are even a couple of settings that Rockstar has already set to Ultra, such as Vehicle Max Texture Quality and Bounding Volume Hierarchy. A surprising number of settings — 18 to be exact — are set to medium or low on PS5 and Xbox Series X​​​​​​​. That number jumps to 38 settings on Xbox Series X that are set to low or medium.​​​​​​​

The conservative presets are of significance for PC gamers. Settings such as Tree, Terrain, Impostor, and Grass Shadows are set to medium and affect draw distance and pop-in.​​​​​​​ Lighting and Ambient Lighting, which influence​​​​​​​ how the game renders background lights such as streetlights and neon signs, are also set to medium across platforms.

Volumetric Lighting​​​​​​​, another setting currently on medium, determines how light is depicted in conditions such as fog and crepuscular rays​​​​​​​. On consoles, aspects like 'god rays' can appear grainy or blocky — especially​​​​​​​ while the camera is in motion.

Even elements that might sound small on paper, like Weapon Textures, could meaningfully change the experience. There's a lot of shooting in this game, even if you play non-lethally; players will stare down the barrel of a gun for much of the game.

Players experiencing GTA 6 on PS5 Pro have slightly more presets set to high than the base platform​​​​​​​, but by and large, a potential PC port​​​​​​​ of the game will likely look much better than its console counterparts, depending on hardware configuration. GTA 6 is no graphics slouch, either — so it's almost hard to fathom how this incredible-looking game is still nowhere near its full potential​​​​​​​.

GTA 6 could theoretically look phenomenal on PC if Rockstar ever releases it on that platform or if the AI vibe coders figure out a port. Here is the other shoe dropping: in order to push GTA 6 to the limit, PC gamers are going to need top-of-the-line hardware​​​​​​​.

Graphics cards like the RTX 5080 or 5090, which could potentially get the game running on high or ultra across the board, cost anywhere from $2,000 to $6,449​​​​​​​. PC gamers will probably want 32 GB of RAM to accommodate​​​​​​​ these graphics cards, and those components are more expensive right now as well. Getting the most impressive version of GTA 6 running could cost many thousands of dollars​​​​​​​, especially if the player is starting a rig from scratch or needs extras like monitors, keyboards, or mice.

Compared to a PC build, the PS5 Pro's higher price tag​​​​​​​ might feel a little less eye-watering​​​​​​​ — if you're able to find one at all. For now, though, all of this is speculative — GTA 6 is not available for PC.

#3441. How Focker In-Law Director John Hamburg Helped Ariana Grande Navigate Her Tricky Character [Exclusive]

When it comes to making a movie sequel like "Focker In-Law," the challenges faced by the returning cast and crew are distinct but dependent on those faced by the newcomers. The former have to try not to repeat themselves, while the latter have to find a way of integrating their work into an already-established milieu. This can be especially tricky when it comes to comedy, as the genre lives and dies on tone and timing. If one or both are off, it can destroy the entire proceedings.

These are the precise challenges that writer/director John Hamburg and star Ariana Grande had to deal with while making "Focker In-Law," the fourth film in the uber-popular "Meet the Parents" franchise. While returning folks like Ben Stiller (as Greg Focker) and Robert De Niro (as Jack Byrnes) could rely on their past work on the property to use as a starting point, Grande had to find a path to her own comedic voice within the film's ensemble. Not making it any easier is the fact that her role is not only key, but complex: She's Olivia Jones, the bride-to-be of Greg's son, Henry (Skyler Gisondo), yet Greg is trepidatious of anyone marrying his boy. Making things more complicated is that Olivia and Greg start off on a bad note that only gets worse, as Greg discovers her past as a former FBI hostage negotiator. This means Grande has to be both a sweet-natured love interest and a potentially conniving antagonist, which is not an easy mix.

When I had the chance to talk with Hamburg about this, he agreed that the challenge was not insignificant. Yet he also revealed how he worked with Grande to craft her character, especially in the editing room, resulting in a great new addition to the Focker saga.

As John Hamburg told me during our chat, it was not lost on himself and the others behind "Focker In-Law" that Ariana Grande had her work cut out for her playing Olivia. Yet, he explained why Grande was so uniquely qualified to handle the challenge:

"We were like, 'Oh my God, she's playing the love interest and the antagonist. What a tight rope.' But honestly, she's so uniquely gifted that I think she's the only person that could really nail that thing where you're kind of scared of her, you're intimidated, but she's also the sweetest, most loving [person]. Her smile lights up a room. Ari brings so much of that energy, but she's just a wonderful actress. So, she could play all those levels."

It turns out that Grande's ability to play multiple levels of a character dovetailed nicely with Hamburg's approach to comedy, which is less about improvisation and more about tweaking the tone and intention of a moment or scene. Hamburg explained how Grande provided him with ample material that he was able to use in post-production:

"[...] When we're filming, I try to get different levels. 'So, okay, maybe try it a little more passive-aggressive, or try it a little more hostile, or say this with a smile,' that kind of thing. And she has so much in her toolbox that she was able to give me so many levels. So, when I got to the editing room, it was like an embarrassment of riches to try while I was crafting her performance."

The wrong person playing Olivia could've sunk the whole film. Fortunately, Hamburg had the right instinct that Grande could handle it.

"Focker In-Law" is currently playing in theaters.

#3440. Ryan Grim Is Bringing the Manosphere Bros and Socialists Together

Anyone still struggling to understand how Bernie Bros and MAGA voters overlap on the political Venn diagram might find answers in Ryan Grim’s audience.

Grim, a veteran journalist and self-described “leftist,” has cultivated a rather politically diverse and incongruous fan base over his two decades in journalism. On election night in Los Angeles earlier this month, a room full of socialists erupted in cheers when Grim appeared on the big screen at the Democratic Socialists of America’s watch party (Grim was a guest that night on Hasan Piker’s livestream). The next day, a friend who religiously listens to Tim Dillon, a podcaster credited with helping Trump win reelection in 2024, and Tony Hinchcliffe, a comedian who performed at a Trump rally that same year, told me that he was also a huge fan of Grim’s.

After working at Politico, HuffPost, and The Intercept, Grim, 48, cofounded Drop Site News, an independent nonprofit news organization, in 2024, and he’s also a cohost on the antiestablishment political podcast Breaking Points. He’s developed a reputation for being an equal opportunity critic of both parties, which Grim says helps explain why people all along the spectrum are attracted to his work. Even Steve Bannon (who called Grim an “intrepid reporter”) and former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz have occasionally thrown compliments his way.

“I think there’s a huge overlap with Breaking Points, Drop Site, and the whole podcast-bro world,” Grim tells Vanity Fair. “It does feel like we’ve basically become the primary news source for the podcast bros, which is not how you would have necessarily understood the world several years ago.”

But lest anyone think that Grim has changed his views to accommodate new fans, his frequent criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza has helped make him a target of Fox News host Mark Levin, who has called into question Drop Site’s nonprofit status.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Grim discusses his unlikely popularity among the podcast bros, why he thinks the Epstein files helped propel Democrats in 2026, why he doesn’t understand the protests against Jerry Seinfeld, and what his favorite jam band, Phish, taught him about tolerance.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: You’ve talked about how being a leftist rather than a Democratic partisan has helped you build credibility with conservatives. Why is that distinction important?

Ryan Grim: [The conservatives] never thought I was a Democratic partisan, because I wasn’t. I think if you have a view of the world, people are willing to say, Okay, that’s his view of the world, and I’m going to metabolize what he’s reporting while taking into account that he has a particular view of the world.

But if you’re a partisan for Democrats or Republicans, that’s different because then you’re playing, like, strategic games with your information, and your view of whether or not something is good or bad changes with whether or not it’s good or bad for Democrats or good or bad for Republicans, rather than being grounded in some type of idea about the world.

And you’ve been criticizing Democrats for decades.

Yeah, I think what frustrates our critics is that they can’t be like, “Oh yeah, well, you didn’t say that when Biden was president or when Obama was president,” and it’s like, “Oh no, in fact, we said this and worse,” because it didn’t matter the color of the jersey. We believed that drone strikes were wrong, or shutting down ACORN is bad, and we’re going to say it no matter who’s in office.

Jeremy [Scahill] and I have been doing this for so long that we have that track record, so I think that has really helped us build that audience across the spectrum. It’s been pretty gratifying to develop that conservative audience. It’s weird sometimes to hear a Steve Bannon or a Matt Gaetz applauding your journalism. But it’s like, hey, that doesn't necessarily mean they agree with us about our conclusions. That’s not what we’re here for. We’re here to do the reporting.

You grew up around a lot of Moral Majority conservatives in rural Maryland, and you’ve said that even though you disagreed with their politics, you didn’t necessarily think they were bad people. Is that something the left has lost sight of?

They were almost universally pretty good people whose views I didn’t share as a young person and don’t now. But that’s just who they are.

I’ve talked to other people who still live in these rural areas, and they’re like, “How do I deal with these people who have these wretched beliefs?” I say, “Just deal with them as people.” They were kind of born believing that, and a lot of them are rethinking things all the time.

You seem to have a lot more patience for people you disagree with than some of your fellow leftists. How do you reconcile that with your own pretty uncompromising politics?

I try to live by the creed of [left-wing political commentator] Michael Brooks. He used to say, “Be ruthless to systems, be kind to people,” and that can be very hard. But to me the most important thing to do is try to understand that people operate within systems, and it is the system that you’re against, not the people.

I think you’re more likely to win converts by understanding what their role is in the system and keeping your criticisms at that systemic level.

I think sometimes people go a little bit crazy. I don’t agree with Jerry Seinfeld’s politics when it comes to Israel, but I don’t understand the value of protesting Jerry Seinfeld. Maybe he’s given some money or something, but like, in general, he’s not a decision-maker. What is the upside in making him a target of protest? That part I don’t understand.

Speaking of people who disagree with you, Mark Levin has been going after Drop Site News’s nonprofit status. How seriously are you taking his efforts?

So if tomorrow Levin succeeded, and we were no longer a nonprofit, we would then carry on as a for-profit supported by our readers.

I know the underlying hostility is he doesn’t like our reporting—he doesn’t want it to exist. But stripping our nonprofit status wouldn’t change that. It would just turn it into a lucrative for-profit company, which I don’t understand. Like, that’s his preferred outcome? That we make a bunch of money doing this? I don’t think it’s very well thought through.

But couldn’t this become a much bigger problem for journalism? There are organizations like ProPublica and The Texas Tribune that could theoretically face similar attacks.

Yes, and certainly the Trump administration has been very publicly saying that it plans to go after the entire nonprofit complex, and everybody from Sierra Club on down, because they consider them to be political enemies.

But [the Trump administration] has also gotten a lot of pushback on this from the conservative-nonprofit world, which is actually much more lucratively funded than the progressive side, because the conservatives have said [Democrats are] going to come for organizations like The Heritage Foundation when Republicans are no longer in power.

Let’s talk about the midterms. Moderates saw the blue wave as a vindication of the party’s affordability-focused strategy, while progressives saw it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda. What was your biggest takeaway?

I think people are overlooking the role that the Epstein files and Trump’s cover-up, in particular, played. That was really a major break that eroded trust from his base and from independents.

We even did a survey right after he launched the war and asked people if they thought he was going to war with Iran to distract, at least in part, from the Epstein scandal. And by a 50-to-42 margin, the majority of the country said yes, he is.

Whether true or not, the Epstein scandal bled into Iran, which then drove up gas prices and created all of this intense anxiety. Meanwhile, Trump is focused on the ballroom, which he’s using to collect bribes.

People believed when they elected him that he was going to drain the swamp, release the files, start no new wars, and focus instead on bringing down prices. That was what people understood he was going to do. And on all four, he just did the exact opposite, in, like, an aggressive, in-your-face, I-don’t-care-about-you kind of way.

You recently discussed a forensic expert’s analysis challenging the official account of Jeffrey Epstein’s death. What interested you about the coverage?

It was certainly interesting that The New York Times was willing to cover it.

Their headline was funny. The one that the Times went with said something like, “Against Conventional Wisdom,” comma, “Forensic Expert Says Epstein Was Murdered.” And I was like, What? What conventional wisdom are you talking about here?

I don’t think the conventional wisdom was challenged there at all.

We live in this interesting world where the public can get to, like, a 70-30, 80-20 belief in something without The New York Times ever giving permission for that belief. And so then when they finally come around to it, like with this article, they say that the story they’re writing goes against conventional wisdom. The conventional wisdom may be wrong, but the conventional wisdom is that he was killed.

What does that say about the state of journalism?

The depressing part, from my perspective, is there’s almost nothing I can report anymore that our readers will admit they’re surprised by, and there’s pretty much nothing you could report on Epstein that would ever live up to what people just assume is true about him.

All right, something considerably more fun: We’re both Phish fans, and I’ve noticed a growing MAGA contingent at their concerts. Does that bother you?

Well, it’s the same audience. You know, they’re just going through changes in their lives. Doesn’t frustrate me at all. All are welcome.

I actually talked to Phish about this in 2002. I met the band after they played at Saturday Night Live. At the time, I was very agitated about the fact that they had not said anything about the Iraq war, and the drummer, Jon Fishman, told me they had said something, one political thing, several years earlier, and they just got flooded with letters from Republican fans who felt hurt.

They’re like, You know what? We’re just not gonna go there anymore. Stop at a stop sign. This is about all we’re gonna say.

And you know what? It’s fine. We don’t need Phish to tell us what they think about the world. They can just create a space for us to think about it.

Phish would not have been able to stop the Iraq war.

But doesn’t some of the anti-Muslim and transphobic rhetoric on the right run counter to the ethos of Phish?

Yeah, but I don’t think any of their audience goes into that.

So you think they’re more fiscal conservatives?

#3439. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

#3438. 5 TV Shows To Watch If You Like Blade Runner 2099

"Blade Runner 2099" has finally premiered on Amazon Prime Video, and if you've been anxiously awaiting this entry in the storied sci-fi franchise inspired by Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" (the basis for the property that launched back in 1982 with Ridley Scott's "Blade Runner"), we've got great news for you. In his review for /Film, Bill Bria praised "Blade Runner 2099" (as was overseen by showrunner Silka Luisa), declaring that Silka "has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud new addition to the saga" and even calling the series "the best sci-fi show in years."

So, what's it about? "Blade Runner 2099," like its film predecessors "Blade Runner" and "Blade Runner 2049," focuses on the interplay between Replicants — an engineered humanoid — and Blade Runners, who are tasked with figuring out who's a human and who's a Replicant and disposing of the latter. (This is what Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard was doing, essentially, in "Blade Runner.") That's where we meet Olwen, a Replicant who's also a Blade Runner — played by Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh — and watch her team up with the human Cora (Hunter Schafer) in a post-revolution world where Replicants now control humans. As Olwen prepares to be retired and Cora pretends to be a Replicant, they look for a group of evil-doing Replicants causing chaos, allowing us to follow their adventures.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are available on Amazon Prime Video as of November 25, but what should you watch when you're finished with the series? I've got some ideas.

Despite ... diminishing returns as J.J. Abrams' show "Alias" reached its endpoint with its fourth season, I still hold this show close to my heart, and fans of the double-crossing and secret identities in "Blade Runner 2099" will definitely love this spy drama. When "Alias" opens, Jennifer Garner's Sydney Bristow is, by all appearances, juggling a high-pressure job at a Los Angeles bank with her graduate studies ... except, the truth is that she doesn't work at a bank but as a spy for what she believes is a covert wing of the CIA called SD-6. When she tells her fiancé the truth about her career and SD-6 has him brutally murdered in their home, Sydney realizes that SD-6 isn't affiliated with United States intelligence but is actually a terrorist cell that's part of a larger structure operating across the world. That's when Sydney becomes a double agent, teams up with her CIA handler (and future husband) Michael Vaughn (Michael Vartan), and works alongside the other mole inside SD-6 ... who turns out to be her estranged father Jack Bristow (a sublime Victor Garber).

The first season of "Alias?" Amazing. The second season of "Alias?" God-tier television, especially "Phase One," the mid-season stunner that secured the coveted post-Super Bowl timeslot in 2003. Season 3 is where things start to go downhill, and in this house, we don't even discuss Season 4. Still, if you want to watch a few very good seasons of a spy drama after "Blade Runner 2099," check out "Alias," which is on Disney+.

"Blade Runner 2099" is many things. "Good" is one of them. "Expensive" is definitely another. You can practically see dollar signs on the screen (the show just looks expensive, and I definitely don't mean that in a bad way). So, if you're looking for another big-budget sci-fi epic that's got plenty of seasons under its belt at this point, consider checking out the Apple TV show "Foundation." Adapted from Isaac Asimov's "Foundation" book series by David S. Goyer and Josh Friedman, "Foundation," which premiered in 2021 and stars Jared Harris and Lee Pace, takes place in a future where living beings live under the control of the Empire, led largely by clones (though it's secretly run by Laura Birn's Lady Demerzel, who controls all of the Empire's leader-clones). Pace plays Brother Day, a middle-era clone of Emperor Cleon I, while Harris plays mathematician Hariton "Hari" Seldon, who can predict the future and serves as a mentor to young prodigy Gaal Dornick (Lou Llobell).

"Foundation" is detailed, sumptuous, and again, looks expensive ... and whatever Apple is spending on this series is beyond worth it. Season 3 concluded in 2025 and the fourth season is already confirmed, so if you watch the show after "Blade Runner 2099," rest assured that there will be more "Foundation" on the way eventually.

The vibes of "Pluribus" and "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't be more different, but if you like the push-and-pull of the interplay between humans and Replicants in the latter, I bet you'll like the dynamic between a hivemind and an unsuspecting woman in the former. Vince Gilligan's first series since "Better Call Saul" reunites him with that show's lead actor Rhea Seehorn and casts her as Carol Sturka, a romance author who's understandably terrified when an alien virus turns almost every human on Earth into part of a hivemind except for her (including her manager/wife Helen L. Umstead, played by Miriam Shor). As one of 12 people immune to said hivemind, Carol is at a total loss and absolutely refuses to follow the pack, which sets up a genuinely hilarious, deeply weird, and riveting series.

"Pluribus" won Seehorn her first-ever Emmy for playing Carol (well-deserved, especially after her years playing "Better Call Saul" lead Kim Wexler), and even though the series boasts a great ensemble, it's more or less a one-woman show as Carol moves through a completely changed Earth and tries to figure out her next move. If you haven't watched "Pluribus" yet and just finished "Blade Runner 2099," check this pick out.

"Blade Runner 2099" is a great series that happens to stand in the shadow of its predecessor, owing largely to the fact that "Blade Runner" is one of the most influential and beloved science fiction films of all time. This is also true of "Andor," an exceptional science fiction series that's part of a larger universe you might be familiar with called the "Star Wars" franchise. Created and run by the great Tony Gilroy, "Andor," a prequel to the movies "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" and "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope," centers on Cassian Andor (Diego Luna), a thief who becomes radicalized against the Galactic Empire over five years and ends up serving as an agent/spy for the Rebel Alliance.

I probably don't need to tell you that "Andor" is one of the best Star Wars projects ever made (this is just established fact), but both "Andor" and "Blade Runner 2099" are given the daunting task of expanding a well-known universe in a way that doesn't feel like a stingy cash grab, and both succeed. If you haven't watched "Andor" yet, you're in for a serious treat. The show only runs for two seasons, but its sophomore outing is regarded as one of the best TV seasons in recent memory by pretty much all of its fans, and it really does pair perfectly with another legacy project like "Blade Runner 2099."

If your favorite thing about "Blade Runner 2099" is the buddy aspect (namely, the way that Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh's characters play against each other), consider another Amazon Prime Video series. Specifically, consider "Fallout," the adaptation of the blockbuster video game series that started airing on the streamer in 2024. The show, created by Graham Wagner and Geneva Robertson-Dworet (with Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy of "Westworld" among the executive producers), centers around Lucy (Ella Purnell), an individual who, like most other people in this world, lives in an underground bunker to avoid the nuclear aftermath of the Great War of 2077 between China and the United States. When Lucy's beloved father Hank is kidnapped suddenly from their home in Vault 33, she decides to venture to the surface and track him down ... and while there, she encounters The Ghoul, a former TV star named Cooper Howard who was mutated by the nuclear blast and is played by Walton Goggins.

Purnell and Goggins are an unexpectedly perfect duo, much like Yeoh and Schafer. So, again, if you're looking for a follow-up series to "Blade Runner 2099" that pairs two unlikely souls together and watches them embark on a journey, try the first two seasons of "Fallout" on Amazon Prime Video. That's also where you can find "Blade Runner 2099" — again, all of Season 1 is streaming now.
