#3413. David Fincher's Rejected Star Wars Movie Pitch Would Have Centered On Two Beloved Franchise Characters

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

His interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:

"I said, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were."

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

"Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened."

Notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:

"I said to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'"

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.

With just over a week before Fortnite Treasure Hunters comes to an end, desperation has set in, as players begin to lose hope of finding the Pirate Shop Access token. This is the most coveted item in Fortnite history because it grants up to 28 days of free Item Shop cosmetics.

The long search for the token has driven players to cheat. Epic Games has managed to catch these cheaters red-handed and has publicly announced that it will be banning them from Fortnite.

The consequences aren't limited to the players who resorted to cheating software. Players who teamed up with the cheater via Squad Fills are the only exception. This measure aims to prevent players from creating a smurf account exclusively for cheating.

The Pirate Shop Access token may be a reward that's almost too good to be true, but it's also extremely rare. The odds of finding the token are low (0.000007273%). Some players have opened over 150,000 chests with no luck, so it can definitely be frustrating to continue on. Players' best bet is to keep searching and collect other treasure from chests along the way.

With Golden Week coming up on Nov. 28, players will at least have increased chances of finding the rare gilded skins. Additionally, the week-long event begins on Saturday, when the final Treasure Hours of the season will be active, cranking up token odds by 1.5x. Fortnite Treasure Hunters ends on Dec. 5, so players still have some time to open chests and get the token before it's vaulted for good.

Ah, the Bulgarian split squat. Feared by many, loathed by most, but loved by personal trainers all over the world. What if I told you that you'd enjoy this lower-body exercise infinitely more if you followed three simple steps to fix up your form?

It's surprisingly easy to make mistakes with this leg-day exercise, and really, it can be adjusted to be more quad-dominant or glute-dominant — but there are clear signs of bad form, and many more people than you'd think end up on the physical therapy couch because of poor lifting mechanics.

To maximize the benefits of this weightlifting exercise, I recommend learning how to do the Bulgarian split squat before bad habits set in. As a trainer, I have a few tips to help you. Scroll on to see if you're making these common mistakes below and my top tips to fix your form fast.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

It's a compound exercise and a part of functional training workouts and strength programs everywhere, helping you build strength and muscle in your glutes, hips, quads, hamstrings and core.

The move requires balance and coordination, while your upper body, core and hips help stabilize you as you move. But people tend to think of this move as more quads than glutes, which isn't exactly the case.

Here's what I see go wrong, and three quick fixes:

In short, you're wasting your time if your form is badly off. And we're busy humans who don't like our time being wasted, right?

Leaning back too far removes tension from the working muscles and overloads your lower back. Keep your torso static and stable — don't hunch or allow your knees to cave inward. That means engaging your core and using the power of your core, glutes and legs to drive movement.

Next, think about your gravity; as I mentioned, keep your back straight and slightly hinge forward to help engage the glutes on your standing leg. If you work with a weight in your opposite hand, this will engage more of the outer glutes, or gluteus medius.

Taking time during the eccentric contraction means slowing down the lowering phase; you can then press upward with power while maximizing tension. It's now thought, due to advances in research, that eccentric contraction is important for muscle growth and braking force.

#3409. Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

Any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the big screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very important to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

This idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

In "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and company have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows users to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

The idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

#3408. ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

One night, after his second child was born, James Gray found himself up late watching C-SPAN coverage of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, and saw something he held onto for years.

“This corporate CEO said, ‘95% of people don’t know there’s a game, and they lose,'” said Gray on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and 1% knows there’s a game and wins. And he said it with evident pride. I thought it revolting.”

The CEO’s words hit home for Gray, showing a “cruel economic system that people can’t control,” where luck, timing, and “having skills that are popular at the right time” decide who wins. Related Stories ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t

“I would love a system where everyone got rewarded, not one that picks winners and losers,” said Gray. “The idea of losers breaks my heart. The film was about my heartbreak over the world’s losers.”

The script for “Paper Tiger” centers on three lead characters, each representing a different side of Gray’s cautionary tale about the dangers of chasing the American Dream. Of his three main characters, Gary (Adam Driver) is best positioned to be one of the “winners.”

“[Gary] is the one person who knows the game, knows how to play it, and just [can’t] live with himself if he makes certain choices that might allow him to, quote-unquote, ‘win,’” said Gray of Driver’s character. “We don’t see that much in movies. We see people who are ‘bad guys’ who make the wrong choice, or ‘good guys’ who make the right choice and then wind up winning for it.”

Gary, the ex-cop turned savvy businessman, presents himself as comfortable crossing that ethical line, but as the story slowly reveals, a strong moral code lies beneath Gary’s slick, tailored suit and wheeler-and-dealer image. It’s a distinction Gray said Driver didn’t fully grasp at first.

“I would go up to [Adam’s] apartment, and we would talk about it, and I remember he was struggling and struggling and struggling, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’” said Gray. “One day in rehearsals, I said, ‘He has only the best intentions all the time.  We have to love him. He always means well. He’s not a sleazeball.’ And Adam went, ‘Oh, I got it.’”

Part of Driver’s problem was that Gary’s latest scheme places his brother Irwin (Miles Teller) and his family in the crosshairs of ruthless Russian mobsters, but Gray warned it was important, for both Driver and the audience, to understand that Gary’s actions weren’t particularly reckless at the time.

“We have the wisdom of 2026 about where organized crime would go in New York, but in 1986, the Russian organization was a totally unknown quantity,” said Gray. “He would not, as a retired police officer, have any knowledge of that.”

In 1986, the Italian mob’s stranglehold on the Gowanus Canal — where Gary is trying to help Irwin score a lucrative contract as an environmental consultant — had been decimated by RICO prosecutions. There was an assumption of a new day dawning, as different immigrant groups began moving into the vacuum left behind by the aggressive prosecution of the Genovese crime family. No one imagined, according to Gray, that one mob would ultimately be replaced by a far more violent and ruthless mob altogether.

“The sadness to me was that the story of immigration in New York at that time was, ‘Oh, these are dissidents, these are engineers, they’re scientists, they’re doctors.’ The expectation wasn’t they were going to set up gasoline, oil, and racketeering. None of that was on the plate,” said Gray, before connecting his point back to Driver. “Adam had the key now that everything was not done for nefarious reasons, that he was trying to bring his brother along. As soon as he could approach it that way, it really opened things up for him.”

Much like the rest of the world, the ruthlessness of the Russian mob would catch Gary by surprise, but it would be how Gary responded to the threat that got Gray’s storytelling juices flowing.

“I was anxious to show a character who you might think would be the one who does the wrong thing, but in fact, does something beautiful in death, which is he sacrifices himself,” said Gray.

This last part is important to Gray, who discussed how his three young adult children constantly complain that “there’s nothing on TV,” despite having more channels and streaming services than ever before. “They always say that to me,” explained Gray, “and what they’re really saying is there’s very little with a streak of grandeur or nobility in it, because there’s a kind of smallness to the storytelling when you don’t have that quality.”

The question then became how to give Driver’s Gary that nobility in death, and build to a third act that gave Gray’s smaller film a sense of grandeur. As with most of his films, Gray drew on his life experiences growing up in Queens, along with great films from the past.

In Howard Beach, Queens, down by JFK Airport, a long stretch of marshes surrounded by tall reeds (phragmites grass) stands in sharp contrast to the urban landscape on the horizon.

“ My brother and I got lost in these very tall weeds,” said Gray. “I was very young. And it’s a recurring nightmare of mine, getting lost in there. And you have no sense of direction. Immediately, it’s extremely disorienting.”

Gray had tried to use the location in his 2007 film “We Own the Night,” but he wasn’t satisfied with the results. In “Paper Tiger,” he cracked how to stage and shoot in the tall grasses, drawing direct inspiration from Masaki Kobayashi’s 1967 “Samurai Rebellion,” resulting in Gary’s last stand being one of the most memorable sequences in recent American movie memory.

A key was how Gray drew meaning from the setting: “I was trying to give Adam Driver‘s character a nobility, but the other part of it is how do you give his character a mythic dimension? And through death, a lot of the times, you can imply transcendence, and I was trying to say that his character was essentially going back to the primordial ooze, that he was returning to something that had nothing to do with the urban landscape.”

On the podcast, Gray talked about how the final scene is stripped of period signifiers, with no glimpse of the urban landscape beyond the weeds, allowing the sequence to “devolve or evolve so that [Gary] would be at peace as he died.” The moment was further brought to life through an effective use of sound, rather than a more traditional score for such an operatic ending. “I just decided this is about him transcending, and so you hear — the track is very weird — birds and insects. There’s the intrusion of aircraft, but it’s also the calm of the wind and the undulation of the phragmites grass. And I just thought that was a way to separate his character and say that he’s reached a kind of mythic status.”

One lesson Gray took from his previous (and in Gray’s mind less successful) attempt to film in the Howard Beach marsh was that he would need more time for the hot and hellish shoot, in which the filmmakers experienced disorientation not unlike Gray did as a kid.

“There’s one shot which is up high where you see these guys converging on Adam’s character. And I remember how difficult the shot was because the minute you put the actor in there and the camera went up here, we couldn’t find the actors in the weeds,” said Gray. “It’s very upsetting and disorienting even to just shoot in that setting, to say nothing of the ticks. But that’s a whole other story.”

“Paper Tiger” expands nationwide on November 25.

#3406. The 25 Best PS5 Games in 2026

What are the best games on PlayStation 5? Hard as it is to believe, the PS5 is — by Sony's own admission — already well past the halfway point of its life-cycle. (It's even time to start thinking about PS6.) It's fair to say that PS5 hasn't been deluged with classics, and the rate of must-play new releases is slower than it has been on previous PlayStations. But it does now have the ultimate killer app: Grand Theft Auto 6.

That aside, the PS5's library has grown to the extent that there's a lot to sort through, and new and old PS5 owners will be wondering what to play. So here’s our living list of the best video games we’ve played on the platform — influenced by the personal tastes of the Polygon team — to be updated as more games come out.

Our latest update to this list on Nov. 25 added Grand Theft Auto 6.

The Polygon staff plays a lot of video games, and everything in this list comes personally recommended by at least one of us. We determined what should be on our list of the best PlayStation 5 games by looking at the quality of each title, but also with an eye for breadth and variety — so you should find something on the list you’ll enjoy, no matter what genres of game you like, how much time you have, or what vibe you are after.

A full six years into the PS5's life, here it is: the game that finally makes sense of this console generation, and makes it all worthwhile. GTA 6 is the best-reviewed game of all time, and you don't have to spend long with it to understand why. It's a deeply engrossing world of astonishing detail, reactivity, and scope, rendered in all the seedy, dayglo glamor that can be mustered by the most expensive video game production of all time. It's a familiarly scattershot satire of modern life in America. But — and it's a huge but — it's also a game of real sensitivity and heart. The central couple of Jason and Lucia are straight-up adorable and Rockstar shows, for the first time in the series' history, a moving willingness to see the best in people. Well... some people. —OW

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Grand Theft Auto 6.

If you're craving a return to the days of Wipeout, when a PlayStation racing game was as likely to involve antigravity sci-fi craft rocketing around at hundreds of miles per hour as realistic cars, then Galactic Racer is the game for you. It also happens to be one of the most innovative racing games in a long time, a much-needed shake-up for a stale genre. It introduces a roguelite structure and build-crafting into both single-player and even multiplayer modes, while keeping it all totally coherent with a very Star Wars fantasy of racing dangerous, rickety hot rods. As a treat, there's a healthy dose of Burnout in there, too. —Oli Welsh

Read Oli Welsh's full review of Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

Here's another classic PlayStation flavor resurrected in an unexpectedly glorious way. As the latest in Bandai Namco's long-running dogfighting air combat series, Ace Combat 8 sounds like a niche known quantity. Try it, however, and you'll be pleasantly surprised again and again: by the sophistication of the controls, the variety of the level design, the meaty length of the campaign, the amazing fidelity of the visuals, and the depth and seriousness of its operatic wartime storyline. —OW

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

The PS5 generation has been a bit short on really great tactics games, but that's all changed with this superb squad strategy game from Bit Reactor, set during Star Wars' Clone Wars era. Many on the team worked on Firaxis' XCOM reboot games, and you can sure tell — this is fine-honed game design full of precision, personality, puzzle-like ingenuity, and just the right amount of unpredictability. Zero Company also makes brilliant use of its setting, compellingly painting a grunt's-eye-view of the collapse of the Republic, and assembling a squad of characters you'll really care about. Especially when you lose them forever in the default permadeath setting. —OW

Read Elijah Gonzalez's full review of Star Wars Zero Company.

It's been a long time since there was an official James Bond game, and a much longer time — almost 30 years, in fact — since there was a really great one. 007 First Light might not attain the legendary status of GoldenEye 007, but it's a very slick and entertaining blockbuster action game that's a lot smarter than it needed to be. The key is an inspired choice of developer in IO Interactive, of Hitman fame. IO's love of open-ended "social stealth" gameplay sneaks its way in between the set-pieces and rounds out a thoroughly satisfying adventure with a unique perspective on a young Bond. —OW

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

It's defiantly not for everyone, but when the planets align, Bungie's take on the extraction shooter genre can be a totally electrifying multiplayer experience. Its asymmetric PvPvE gameplay can be hard to get your head around, never mind brutally unforgiving, but for intensity and drama it can hardly be matched, and Bungie is to be commended for including interesting solo as well as group roles. On top of this, you have intriguingly deep sci-fi world-building, Bungie's world-class gamefeel — 25 years on from Halo, there are still no more satisfying guns to shoot in gaming — and absolutely stunning art direction, realising one a compellingly chilling future. —OW

Read Corey Plante's impressions of Marathon.

You can accuse this sequel to Supergiant Games' smash hit roguelike action game of overcomplicating the pure brilliance of the first Hades, and we did. But really this is quibbling with something that's very close to perfection. The combat is still crisp and thrilling, the randomized boons are still exquisitely balanced, the see-saw between progression and setback on each run is still perfectly judged, and the languid, sexy bickering of Supergiant's take on the pantheon of Greek mythology is still gloriously characterful and thirsty. Simply the best that indie gaming has to offer. —OW

Capcom has completed a swift one-two punch in early 2026 by following Resident Evil Requiem with an unexpected gem of a sci-fi action game. Like all of Capcom's best work, Pragmata is both a slick, modern blockbuster and steeped in deep, old-school video game vibes. It's a cinematically ambitious game about fatherhood and the AI threat. But also you're a dude in a spacesuit shooting robots on a moon base, eking out your resources and testing your reflexes between save points.

This is a time-honored template (albeit one that makes for a pleasant gear-change in the here and now). Capcom mixes it up with Diana, your childlike android companion, who disrupts both the storytelling and the gameplay in interesting ways. She sweetly draws the best out of the protagonist, Hugh, while potentially fooling both Hugh and the player that she's any different from the AI army they combat. And her hacking ability, which plays out as a grid-based minigame, is Pragmata's chief gameplay innovation; it blends surprisingly compelling quickfire puzzles into the third-person shooting to brilliant effect — so much so that, when you earn the ability to bypass it, you'll probably choose not to. Pragmata plays solidly, looks sharp, and most importantly, feels fresh. It's a class act. —OW

Read Austin Manchester's full review of Pragmata.

It’s a bold move, on the part of Remedy Entertainment, to actually make a decade-late sequel to a game that defined the studio, but whose ambitions it has arguably outgrown in the years since — particularly in its stunning, architectural action game Control. Might a trip back to Alan Wake’s spooky woods, so obviously haunted by the ghosts of Stephen King and David Lynch, not feel like a step back? Hardly. What Remedy created by bringing all its experience to bear on its most beloved creation is nothing short of a survival horror masterpiece, as well as a meta mystery about its own creation.

Horror author Alan is joined by a co-protagonist, FBI agent Saga Anderson, who’s investigating a case linked to Alan’s disappearance over a decade earlier. Using this dual setup — impressively, you can fluidly switch between Alan’s and Saga’s stories essentially at your discretion — Remedy works outward from the original game’s premise, twisting it into a methodical detective thriller one moment and a reality-bending cosmic horror the next. Alan Wake 2 announces the start of a new generation of blockbuster horror gaming. —OW

Read Toussaint Egan’s full review of Alan Wake 2.

One of the most exciting gaming stories of 2024 has been the elevation of Team Asobi, makers of a series of charming tech demos, to the top flight of Sony’s in-house developers with Astro Bot. Expanding on the free pack-in game Astro’s Playroom, intended as a demo for the capabilities of the DualSense controller, Astro Bot is a dazzling, full-fledged, tour de force platform game capable of standing toe-to-toe with some of Nintendo’s greatest — and it’s surely the best platformer Sony has ever released.

Astro Bot is many things at once. It’s a stunning technical showcase, from the sheen of its ray-traced surfaces to the tippy-tap of the adorable Astro’s footfalls rendered in the DualSense’s haptics and speaker. It’s a nonstop riot of invention that keeps throwing new ideas, gizmos, slapstick interactions, hilarious bosses, and tortuous challenges at you. And — with its hundreds of collectible bots dressed up as PlayStation game characters — it’s a wholehearted, even moving celebration of PlayStation history in the brand’s 30th anniversary year that takes particular care to honor the many wild creations of Japan Studio, the now sadly defunct in-house developer Team Asobi used to call home. It’s poignant to reflect that the time of such creative PlayStation games as Ico, LocoRoco, and PaRappa the Rapper is passed. But it’s joyful to realize that Astro and Team Asobi are here to keep that spirit alive into the future. —OW

Read Oli Welsh’s full review of Astro Bot.

#3405. Avatar Fans Just Got Some Good News About The Franchise's Future At Disney

"Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

Was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

There's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is currently working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils."

Cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash."

James Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

The "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:

"There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course."

What about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

Quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is currently scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

#3403. Avengers: Secret Wars Setting Confirmed By Marvel, Spoiling Doomsday

It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a new planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

The Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

The first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

This second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars."

Asked to comment further, Feige said, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

None of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a big shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for new characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

We know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter."

Whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a big screen visit to Battleworld.

#3402. Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z

Lauren Ambrose sounds almost embarrassed to admit that she was puzzled the first time she read the script for Nick Payne’s “The Unbelievers.” “I was like, ‘Oh my God, what is this? I don’t understand this at all,'” Ambrose told IndieWire, scrunching up her face in a mask of bewilderment. “What’s he getting at?”

The drama, which is wrapping up its limited run at the Manhattan Theatre Club this month, is elliptical, moving backward and forward in time as it follows Miriam’s search for her missing son, Oscar. That description sounds like a thousand thrillers, but “The Unbelievers” resists easy classification — it’s a narratively daring story, overflowing with ideas about grief and faith and family. Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future

It was only after doing a workshop for the play that Ambrose discovered that what she initially found so alienating about “The Unbelievers” was actually its greatest strength. “There’s a lot to talk about, and a lot to parse, and a lot to think about, and it’s highly interpretable and analyzable, and I think that’s actually a marker of good art is that it can be interpreted in many ways,” Ambrose said over Zoom, hours before she was set to take the stage again.

The role of Miriam is almost Everest-like in its difficulty. As the years pass without any sign of Oscar — not knowing if he’s been kidnapped or murdered or ran away — Miriam becomes more obsessed, more unmoored by the lack of resolution. That strains her relationship with her two daughters and Oliver’s father, who are processing their grief in different ways and worry that Miriam is growing fanatical in her insistence that he may still be out there.

“It’s fun in a perverse way to go on this crazy journey every night,” Ambrose said. “There are all these wild turns. It’s tiring vocally. My body hurts, my neck is messed up. But it’s amazing to get to play a part like this. You just have to throw yourself off a cliff.”

Ambrose made a name for herself in films like “Can’t Hardly Wait” and on “Six Feet Under,” where she played Claire Fisher, a rebellious dreamer growing up in her family-run funeral home. The show debuted in 2001 on HBO, where it aired alongside “The Sopranos” and “Sex and the City” at the peak of the cable channel’s cultural supremacy. Decades later, “Six Feet Under” has been rediscovered on streaming by Gen Z, giving it an unexpected surge in popularity.

“It was a golden age,” Ambrose said. “We were making these hour-long films each week. And HBO was so open and supportive of creative people. The attitude was, if you want to try something, try it. There weren’t algorithms determining everything. That freedom is palpable with the series, so I think that’s why it’s resonating and why it’s being embraced by this new generation.”

Ambrose remains in demand on the big and small screen, recently appearing on another water-cooler hit, Showtime’s “Yellowjackets.” But she’s made a point of returning to the stage throughout her career, appearing on Broadway in “Exit the King” and “Awake and Sing!,” as well as earning a Tony Award nomination playing Eliza Doolittle in a revival of “My Fair Lady.”

“I love the stage — I love it so much,” Ambrose said. “I love a rehearsal room. It’s my favorite place in the world. It’s where you’re figuring it out and making connections. But a play is always a living thing. We’ve opened ‘The Unbelievers,’ but I haven’t stopped my work of trying to scavenge around and figure out this mysterious character.”

Hand tools and bits are a big part of a well-appointed home tool set, and a part that is often overlooked until a third or fourth trip to the hardware store. Saving some money on these tools will also save you time and aggravation while you’re working on your DIY projects.

#3400. How Blade Runner 2099 Took Inspiration From Denis Villeneuve's Legacy Sequel [Exclusive]

It's impossible enough to have to live in the shadow of an unabashed classic of cinema, so just imagine dealing with two of them. There aren't many who would have a bad word to say about Ridley Scott's original "Blade Runner (well, except for those unfortunate critics who dismissed it upon release), but Denis Villeneuve's highly-acclaimed sequel "Blade Runner 2049" ain't too shabby, either. Now, Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" series has the added responsibility of picking up the story where its beloved predecessors left off ... along with all the pressure that comes with that.

For showrunner Silka Luisa, this could've required one of two different approaches: stay suffocatingly faithful to the look and feel and tone of the two films or purposefully set off in the opposite direction. Well, in this case, how about a secret third option instead? During a recent press junket for "Blade Runner 2099," I spoke with Luisa over Zoom about where this show fits in next to its movie kin and how it finds its own niche amid a much wider world:

"I knew we were definitely going to have an opportunity to lay our own track, because — it's right in the title, the fact that you're so many years past 2049, it gives you enough space to really carve out your own identity."

Impressively, Luisa looked to Villeneuve's 2017 movie to figure out the ideal way to do just that. "What was so fantastic about what Denis did with '2049' was, he didn't just rehash what Ridley had done," the showrunner told me. "He really created his own take on 'Blade Runner' that is very much his aesthetic. But it still felt like an evolution of Ridley's conversation." In effect, the key was to thread that very tricky needle for "2099."

When it comes to the recent trend of legacy sequels that have dominated the last decade or so of franchise filmmaking, it can certainly feel like we can count the worthwhile ones on just one or two hands. Fortunately, for Silka Luisa and her creative team on "Blade Runner 2099," Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049" is basically the poster child for legacy sequels done right. Rather than simply retread all the same ground as before (looking at you, "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens"), "Blade Runner 2049" moved the story forward and took some seriously big risks along the way.

According to Luisa, this gave her all the permission she needed to follow in its footsteps and take things in bold new directions with her show. "That freed us up in a lot of different ways, because it meant we weren't just beholden to repeating the same thing over and over again," she explains. One massive wrinkle in the Prime Video series is the fact "Blade Runner 2099" takes place after a Replicant uprising has shaken up the status quo, putting humans at the bottom of the food chain for once. It's a strange dynamic that our two main characters Olwen (the Replicant Blade Runner played by Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (the human posing as a Replicant played by Hunter Schafer) are forced to navigate throughout the season.

As fans tune in, they can rest assured in the knowledge that the series is taking its cues from one of the most ambitious and boundary-pushing legacy sequels of them all. You could do a lot worse than that. All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are now on Prime Video.

#3399. 'Avengers: Doomsday' Is Making Sure Patrick Stewart Gets a Proper Sendoff

The late X-Men and Star Trek star will receive a special tribute in December’s Marvel blockbuster

Patrick Stewart's final on-screen performance will arrive in December's Avengers: Doomsday, and Marvel is making sure the late actor receives a fitting farewell.

Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige and directors Anthony and Joe Russo are planning to include a tribute to Stewart in the upcoming superhero blockbuster, according to a new interview with Variety. Stewart died on Oct. 29 at age 86 following a brief battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

The actor had already completed filming for Doomsday, in which he reprises his iconic role as Professor Charles Xavier for the ninth and final time. Speaking to Variety, Feige revealed that Stewart's last day on set was an emotional occasion, with the actor delivering a speech to the crew.

"He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew," Feige said. "We didn't know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was."

Anthony Russo also recalled how difficult filming had become for Stewart as he struggled with his health. Despite the challenges, the actor remained committed to delivering his performance.

"For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional," Russo said.

Although principal photography has wrapped, Feige said Marvel is now figuring out how to properly honor its longtime collaborator.

"We're long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us," Feige told Variety. "We're looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend."

The tribute will carry particular significance given Stewart's history with the X-Men franchise. He first played Professor X in 2000's X-Men, becoming one of the defining faces of the superhero series alongside Ian McKellen's Magneto. The two actors will reunite in Doomsday, with Joe Russo revealing that their characters share an emotional scene about forgiveness.

"In a lot of ways, Xavier's the conscience in the movie," Russo said. "He has a lovely scene with Ian McKellen, who's his best friend, in the film. It's a very emotional scene about forgiveness, and I think very resonant in the wake of his passing."

Stewart's death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fans, fellow actors, and gaming communities. Players of No Man's Sky, for example, began naming planets and entire star systems after the actor, with some creating virtual memorials inspired by his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on Dec. 18.

#3397. Quentin Tarantino Did More Than Just Write The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth

Quentin Tarantino has returned to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" (why not read our review of the new movie here?). But this time, while Tarantino penned the script, he isn't in the director's chair. Instead, he's handed directing duties over to his pal David Fincher (who is ending his exclusive deal with Netflix with the film). Tarantino might not be behind the camera, but he still has a presence in the film, and it echoes something he did in "Hollywood" as well.

Early in "Cliff Booth," we're introduced to Charlie Peters, a hot-tempered TV star played by Scott Caan. To speed-run us through Charlie's successful career, we're given a little montage of his various roles, and that montage is narrated by none other than Tarantino, whose very recognizable voice provides some humorous details about Charlie's work.

Fans of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" will recall that Tarantino also provided narration in that movie, too. He actually wasn't the only narrator, either, because during one scene, Kurt Russell, who plays a stuntman named Randy in that film, also provides a little narration. As for Tarantino, he also voiced some crucial narration during a pivotal scene in "The Hateful Eight."

In fact, the filmmaker has a history of popping up in his movies, either via a voice cameo or a physical appearance. He has a pretty significant role in "Reservoir Dogs," makes a memorable cameo in "Pulp Fiction," gets to use an abysmal Australian accent in "Django Unchained," has his voice heard during a movie playing in "Inglourious Basterds" (and also plays a corpse in the film), plays a bartender in "Death Proof," portrays one of the members of the Crazy 88 gang in "Kill Bill," and lends his voice to an answering machine in "Jackie Brown."

So while "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may not technically be a Quentin Tarantino movie, it still feels like one, right down to the obligatory cameo.

#3395. ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 27, 2026 during the 2026 AFI Film Festival. The film is available to stream on Netflix today.]

There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa. Related Stories Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

Perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a big game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

Individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

But then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

Still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something important), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

Netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.

#3394. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

Cats make a wonderful household pet, but cleaning their litter box is not so much fun, which is why I’ve tried several automatic litter boxes over the years to see if any could make it less of a chore.

The latest model I’ve been using, the Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit, is the most expensive, and largest one I’ve yet brought into my house. I — or more specifically my cats — have been using it for about two months, and they seem to have taken to it well. However, before you spend upwards of $600 on this thing, there’s a few things you should know first.

This self-cleaning litter box is designed for cats up to 25 pounds, works with a variety of litter, a 12L waste bin with odor control, and has an app that lets you monitor your cats' weight.

This litterbox is huge. The box it came in was larger than ones I got with microwaves. Measuring 23.62 x 28.07 x 27.44 inches, you’re definitely going to need a lot of space for it, so I would not recommend it if you’re planning to put it in a smallish bathroom.

The HomeRun Pet litterbox looks kind of like a cement mixer. The main part of the box is a large drum with a hole in its side; this is where your cat enters and does its business. When they’re done, and after a minute or two, the litterbox rotates this section to empty the waste into a small storage bin on the side, and then refreshes the clean litter from a reservoir.

To the right of this main drum is a reservoir into which you pour fresh litter. The machine will draw from this reservoir to replenish the main tray.

No more scooping! When the machine empties itself, waste is funneled into a small bin on the right side, which you line with an included plastic bag. When the bag is full — you'll get an alert on your phone — you simply pull the bin out and remove the bag. Replacement bags cost $35 for a pack of 60. With two cats, we’ve had to replace the bag once every two weeks or so.

There’s actually two trays; a second one, which sits directly below the drum, can be used if you want to completely empty the litter box. And, every piece of the litter box that could possibly get dirty can be removed and washed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This being a “smart” cat litter box, you get all sorts of updates via the HomeRun app — when it needs to be emptied, when you need to add new litter, how long your cats take, and how many times they go per day.

One interesting feature of the HomeRun Pet is that it has a built-in scale, so you can keep tabs on your cats’ weight. I initially had to wait until each of mine used the box to figure out which was which, but after that, it would tell me which cat had gone, and when. Of course, if your cats are very close in weight, it might have trouble telling the difference. If that’s the case, you can adjust the weight error value, so it can better distinguish between multiple pets.

The app also lets you customize all sorts of things, like the type of litter you’re using, cleaning schedule, and even “kitten protection,” to prevent the device from activating automatically.

In order to use the HomeRun, your cat has to step up about a foot to get inside the opening; knowing how a cat of mine had trouble walking in his later years, I highly doubt he’d have been able to make it up. Something like the PetSafe Smart Self-Cleaning Litterbox would make more sense (and it’s a lot cheaper and takes up a lot less space).

The Homerunpet Self Cleaning Cat Litter Box Kit is not a small investment; even with Black Friday sales, you’re still going to spend $659 at Amazon on this thing. And, it takes up a lot of space. However, it does make cleaning up after your cat incredibly convenient - just slide open a tray, remove a bag, and you’re all set. Is that worth the price of a nice TV? That’s for you to decide.

#3392. Mckenna Grace Confirms How Much More Tragic Maysilee’s Sunrise On The Reaping Death Should’ve Been

Warning: Contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping!There are plenty of deaths in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, including the fall of Mckenna Grace's Maysilee Donner. She was one of four tributes reaped from District 12, and despite an icy relationship with Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) at first, they become close allies throughout the 50th Hunger Games. This partnership ended once Maysilee died in Sunrise on the Reaping.

As one of the movie's biggest characters, the death hit audiences and Haymitch hard. It's already considered one of Hunger Games' most tragic deaths throughout the entire franchise. Maysilee's fighting spirit endeared her to audiences and her fellow District 12 tributes. And even though Sunrise on the Reaping cut a key Maysilee scene that better explains why she was killed, it was still impactful.

After helping Haymitch burn through bushes to reach the edge of the arena, Maysilee goes her separate way, only for President Snow and the Gamemakers to send bird mutts after her. Armed with razor-sharp beaks, they attack Maysilee in an open field, leaving Haymitch to hear her scream and try to come to her rescue. His efforts fall short, leaving her to die in his arms.

However, as Hunger Games book readers know, Maysilee's death is much more gruesome on the page compared to the movie. It's since been confirmed that there was a much more book-accurate version of Maysilee's death scene that had to be changed to maintain a PG-13 rating, with Grace offering a behind-the-scenes look at the original intent. Check out a comparison of the final and initial designs below:

Suzanne Collins wrote a rather graphic death for Maysilee in Sunrise on the Reaping. The book describes Maysilee kneeling on the ground as the mutts attack, and they've already "taken their toll" by the time Haymitch sees her. The novel then describes that "blood blossoms from her cheek, her chest, the palm of her hand" as a result of their attacks, with one final mutt "driving its beak through her throat."

Grace's BTS image shows that Sunrise on the Reaping planned to bring that brutal, agonizing demise to screen. Grace's face is covered in cuts from the mutts that more accurately show the damage they dealt in the book. There is even a large vertical cut in the middle of her neck, which the final bird would have been responsible for. The original design conveys the same violent death the book had.

However, this was not how Maysilee's death happened in the movie. The film leaves much of the birds' damage to Maysilee for viewers to imagine rather than see. Her final look features far fewer cuts and a lot less blood. Sunrise on the Reaping pulled back on the violence and gore, which is disappointing considering how visceral and effective Maysilee's death is in the book.

The core cause of Sunrise on the Reaping's change is the film's desire to be PG-13. The MPA has strict guidelines about blood and violence, which this prequel already pushed the boundaries of by being the first Hunger Games movie to earn warnings of bloody images and strong violence. Maysilee's death is one of the many changes the movie had to make to avoid an R-rating.

Director Francis Lawrence confirmed in an interview with Kevin McCarthy the intent to have a more violent death for Grace's character, including showing the blood spilling from her neck wound. He noted that it "killed" him to scale back the sequence, but his hands were tied. All the Hunger Games movies have been PG-13, and Sunrise on the Reaping's box office shows why they don't venture into R territory.

The prequel's PG-13 approach affected more than just Maysilee. Louella's death is much more gruesome in the book. Sunrise on the Reaping even cut Wellie's death, which came in the form of a brutal decapitation in the book. Collins wrote the prequel as the most violent and disturbing entry, but the movie held back across the board to keep the familiar franchise rating.

Now, fans will likely never get to see Maysilee's original death from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Its violent content would make it a surprising choice for a deleted/alternate scene as part of the film's digital and physical release, especially since there's a chance viewers could like the original version more, making the change tougher to accept.

#3391. ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain

In March 2009, a train crash kills 46 people near a picturesque village nestled deep within the Italian Alps. In the present day, an alcoholic gym teacher named Sergio (Michele Riondino) — nursing some recent grief of his own — is relocated to Remis, only to find that the surviving townspeople have never been happier, despite the shared tragedy that would seem to overshadow their lives.

It’s uncanny. It’s disturbing. It’s what Sergio wants for himself more than anything in the world. And he’s told that all he has to do to make the pain go away is to hug “The Holy Boy” mentioned in the English title of Paolo Strippoli’s third feature, a slick and effectively spine-tickling horror movie about the harm sown into people convinced they can avoid their own hurt. (It’s also one hell of a calling card for the young Italian director, whose recent festival hit “The Spiral” will receive an Oscar-qualifying release later this year, and an English-language remake sometime after that). Related Stories ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z

For a time, Sergio becomes one of those people. When he first arrives in Remis, sobbing in his car as it chugs up the curvy mountain roads, it feels like a cruel joke that the surly ex-Judo champion has been relocated to a place known as “The Valley of Smiles.” He’s a belligerent asshole to the kids in his P.E. class, acts violently toward the beautiful waitress (Romana Maggiora Vergano as Michela) at the local bar, and generally brings a “Bad Santa” energy to a town with more of a “Pleasantville” vibe.

But from the start, it’s clear Remis hides a secret darkness — a darkness so deep that none of the residents can see clearly that they live in a horror film. It isn’t normal for a weasel-eyed man to stand in the bushes and glare at the village high school all day. It isn’t normal for everyone to meet in a barn on the outskirts of town in the middle of the night and participate in a vaguely Catholic ritual that sees them all line up for a chance to lay their hands on a sullen 15-year-old kid (Giulio Feltri as Matteo). It isn’t normal for them to feel like they might go insane, or worse, if they go too long without his touch. Give people a panacea for their pain, and they’ll do anything to keep it, logic be damned.

Of course, logic is hardly the only thing that’s damned in “The Holy Boy,” whose concussive soundtrack, broadly demonic symbology (e.g., dropped coins transforming into bloody egg yolks), and genre-inflected visual motifs (lots of upside-down camerawork and clever uses of soft focus) help consecrate this high-altitude “Twilight Zone” story’s rather literal approach to elevated horror. But Strippoli’s script, co-written by Jacopo Del Giudice and Milo Tissone, isn’t content to settle for mere social allegory, even if the movie tacks harder in that direction with every new detail we learn about Matteo’s effect on the people who touch him. On the contrary, the film’s excellent second act — during which Sergio is fully seduced by the town’s healing power and even settles into a sexual relationship with Michaela — leverages its premise in service of a tenderly ominous character study.

Closeted, sanctified, and at the mercy of a purpose that he never chose for himself, Matteo struggles to see his gift as a miracle; if anything, he worries that it’s more like a curse in disguise. It was, perhaps, easier for him to live with (and be used for) when he was a child, but the self-determination of teenage desire has complicated his relationship to the power he embodies. It’s not just that nobody understands Matteo, or cares to — he also struggles to understand himself. If the local bully is so mean to him at school every day, why does Matteo touch himself when he thinks about him at night? The answer may be obvious, but it doesn’t bring peace to the boy’s tormented heart, which pumps with a pain no one else in town allows themselves to feel. Not even Sergio, whose curiosity toward Matteo proves humanizing — and the basis for a real friendship — even as he grows addicted to the child’s power himself.

It’s here, between the smiling eeriness of its first act and the somewhat “Akira”-coded psychic collapse of its third, that “The Holy Boy” settles into its skin-crawling purpose. The film is at its most confident and secure as a “Thelma”-like coming-of-age story that weaponizes teenage growing pains against the world at large, as Matteo’s limitless potential is poisoned by the unmet needs of the wanting and selfish people around him. In his own way, and despite his best efforts, Sergio is such a person himself, even if he’s still close enough to his own heartache to see Matteo more clearly than most.

But Strippoli is only interested in Sergio as a way to push back against Matteo’s power (and therefore escalate things to the wild places they go before arriving at the film’s satisfying final beat). A richer pas de deux that probes deeper into the grown man’s loss — and his rather complicated history of fathering teenage boys — is gradually sacrificed at the altar of social commentary.

Religion and fascism are Strippoli’s most obvious targets, but “The Holy Boy” is wary of anything that people rely on to absolve them of their pain, and of how the things we turn to for comfort are liable to control us the moment we convince ourselves to believe in miracles. Touched by evil from the moment it starts, Strippoli’s film never invites the kind of faith from its audience that it abuses from its characters en masse, but I didn’t have any trouble believing the moral of its twisted sermon: Keep your pain alive, as it might be the only thing protecting you from something so much worse.

“The Holy Boy” will be available to stream on Shudder starting Friday, November 27.
