#3390. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

#3389. ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

What does “Michael Caine” sound like in the freezing cold? We’re about to find out with the just-announced release of “The Trip to the Northern Lights,” which is the reunion of Steve Coogan, Rob Brydon, and director Michael Winterbottom for what is the fifth installment of “The Trip” franchise of miniseries/movies.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio picked up the U.S. rights to the fifth “Trip” film (IFC has released all four of the other films into theaters in the U.S.) and will release it theatrically on April 9, 2027. It will have been nearly seven years since the release of the last feature, and it sees Brydon now at 60 and Coogan at 59, so we’re guessing their ages may have made their wit and appetites even more ornery since. Related Stories ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

“The Trip” movies are known for their food and travel porn as much as they are for their litany of impressions between Coogan and Brydon playing versions of themselves, but this one turns that concept on its head slightly by sending Coogan and Brydon up north, this time throughout Scandinavia, including Sweden and some islands in Norway, all in search of some other fine food and wry conversation.

The first look at the movie above sees the duo in ridiculously huge parkas in the snow as guided by some sled huskies. Try doing your best Bane impression at 10 below zero.

“We are very happy to be back on the road with IFC. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first ‘Trip’ all those years ago. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights‘ takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle,” Winterbottom said. “I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.”

“The Trip” franchise began all the way back in 2011, and since then the films have spanned trips in England, Italy, Spain, and Greece. As has been the case with all of the installments, they’ve been miniseries airing on TV in England but then edited into films for the U.S. release. The first movie made $3.9 million worldwide across several re-releases, “The Trip to Italy” in 2014 made $6.1 million, 2017’s “The Trip to Spain” made $1.9 million, and “The Trip to Greece” in the COVID-addled summer 2020 still managed to make $259K worldwide.

All four of the “Trip” movies are currently available for streaming on Sun Now, which is the streamer owned by Independent Film Company parent AMC Global Media.

“The Independent Film Company is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each new trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” said Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Vice President of Acquisitions and Production.

“Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan, and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights’ advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio.

The film is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Company and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

Executive producers are Winterbottom, Coogan, Brydon, Alex Moody, Josh Sapan, Tristan Whalley, Paul Wiegard. “The Trip to the Northern Lights” is a Revolution Films, Baby Cow, and Small Man Production in association with Sky Studios.

Deadline first reported the news of the acquisition.

#3388. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

#3387. 9 Years Later, Matt Reeves’ Sci-Fi Masterpiece Returns to Streaming

In the last few years, Matt Reeves has become widely known and celebrated as a director thanks to his work on The Batman starring Robert Pattinson. Production on The Batman Part II is set to come to a close soon, and now that Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, there’s doubt that he will continue as Batman after the film has been released. The future of the franchise was already in doubt after a personal matter forced Reeves to step back from shooting the sequel during its final stages, but the studio brought in Steven Soderbergh to finish principal photography in Reeves’ stead. Like many filmmakers, Reeves has given a large chunk of his career to a singular property, but the demand for more out of his Batman project is so great that fans have shown they’re willing to wait extended periods for another film — the sequel isn’t coming to theaters until 2028.

In the late 2000s, Matt Reeves exploded onto the scene as a director thanks to his work in Cloverfield, the 2008 disaster epic that’s currently streaming for free on Pluto TV. However, in 2014, Reeves helmed what many would argue is still the best film of his career, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes, the sci-fi thriller starring Andy Serkis. He returned three years later to direct the final film in the trilogy, War for the Planet of the Apes, which grossed nearly $500 million at the box office against a $150 million budget. Nine years later, the film has found a streaming home on HBO Max, where it has recently surged into the top 10 over the last week.

The first Planet of the Apes movie in the reboot series, which stars James Franco, follows Caesar as he becomes conscious and aware, breaking out of captivity and moving on to live as a free ape in the wild. The sequel sets the stage for the giant war between humans and apes in the trilogy-capper, which holds scores of 94% from critics and 84% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes. The film also features plenty of other stars you might recognize, such as Woody Harrelson and Steve Zahn.

Check out War for the Planet of the Apes on HBO Max and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Matt Reeves' future projects, including The Batman Part II.

#3386. Marvel Announces New Spider-Man Noir Series Launching In February 2027

Marvel's grittiest Spider-Man returns in 2027 with a brand-new series. Apart from being Marvel’s most recognizable and lucrative character worldwide, Spider-Man has also evolved into a self-sustaining multimedia franchise with multiple fan-favorite protagonists. Alongside Peter Parker’s classic adventures, Miles Morales has become a generational icon in his own right across comics, video games, and animated movies and shows. Miguel O’Hara, Gwen Stacy, and Ben Reilly each have built their own mythos and fan communities. The concept of the Spider-Verse allows multiple Spider-heroes from drastically different eras and backgrounds to thrive simultaneously as standalone and crossover stars.

Among those breakout variants, Spider-Man Noir has enjoyed various surges in popularity over the past fifteen years. Following his 2009 introduction in the four-part miniseries Spider-Man Noir #1, Marvel's 1930s Peter Parker took a leap into video game territory in Beenox’s 2010 video game Spider-Man: Shattered Dimensions, which introduced millions of players to his shadow-stealth combat and Great Depression-era mystery aesthetic. Eight years later, Nicolas Cage’s deadpan performance in 2018’s Oscar-winning Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse transformed him into an instant pop-culture phenomenon, momentum that culminated in Cage reprising his role in Prime Video and MGM+’s 2026 live-action series Spider-Noir.

While not as present as many of his fellow Spider-heroes, Spider-Man Noir continues to take the spotlight across different media.

Unveiled during Marvel’s Spider-Man panel at New York Comic Con 2026, a brand-new five-issue Spider-Man: Noir limited series presents a thrilling comic-book follow-up to Nicolas Cage’s one-season Prime Video live-action series, though not in the same continuity. Acclaimed crime novelist and comic writer Alex Segura, best known for his award-winning mystery novel Secret Identity and his work on Marvel's Spider-Society, teams up with artist Farid Karami, known for his work on Venom: Lethal Protector II, Daredevil, Punisher, and Avengers. This new volume returns to the canonical Earth-90214 continuity, following the classic 1930s Depression-era Peter Parker right when his personal life finally seems headed in a brighter direction.

Peter's brief moment of peace vanishes when a mysterious underworld relic, a perilous femme fatale, and the sudden disappearance of his new girlfriend's former partner pull him back into Manhattan’s fog-drenched criminal abyss. Tempted by the promise of boundless dark power while hunting down a ruthless killer, Spider-Man Noir faces a classic hard-boiled moral test. Remarkably, Segura and Karami’s investigation marks a major milestone for Earth-90214 lore with the introduction of Venom Noir, who brings Marvel’s iconic symbiote mythos into the 1930s Noir universe for the very first time.

Marvel's upcoming Spider-Man: Noir miniseries arrives as a direct follow-up to Spider-Man Noir: The Gwen Stacy Affair, yet Marvel has left the wider Earth-90214 comic book setting largely untouched for over a decade. The Marvel Noir universe transformed iconic heroes into grounded 1930s archetypes, including a non-mutant X-Men Noir team led by detective Charles Xavier, a pulpy globe-trotting adventurer Iron Man Noir, and a scarred circus-act Punisher Noir. But aside from brief multiversal cameos in Spider-Verse and Web-Warriors crossovers, most of these standout incarnations have sat dormant since their original 2009–2010 miniseries concluded.

Spider-Man himself may have more memorable lines than Uncle Ben's "with great power comes great responsibility."

Now is the perfect time to revive the full Marvel Noir imprint, as DC’s massive critical and commercial triumph with Absolute Batman and the wider Absolute Universe demonstrates how well modern readers embrace bold, self-contained reinventions of classic heroes. Earth-90214 thrives on visceral street-level period atmosphere and moral ambiguity. Nearing two decades of history, Marvel's Noir universe still has plenty in store when it comes to grounded detective work and monster-movie terror. With Venom making his Spider-Man: Noir debut in February 2027, Marvel has the ideal springboard to relaunch X-Men Noir, Daredevil Noir, and Iron Man Noir as a relevant line capable of rivaling DC’s hottest alternate-universe titles.

#3382. ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March

“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” a Japan-set take on police decadence, will open in North America on March 5, 2027. Neon, the Oscar-winning studio behind “Anora” and “Parasite,” is distributing the film.

Directed by Takashi Miike, the Japanese auteur behind “Audition” and “13 Assassins,” “”Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” stars Shun Oguri (“Godzilla v. Kong”), Lily James (“Pam and Tommy”), and WWE star Liv Morgan. It follows a veteran police detective Yabuki (Oguri), who is struggling with drug addiction, gambling debts, and guilt over past misdeeds, as he chases a shadowy killer tied to organized crime through Tokyo. His case ends up intersecting with that of an American FBI agent (James), who’s hunting a missing tourist (Morgan). Related Stories ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain

The film had its world premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival, where it earned mixed notices, with some reviewers faulting it as overstuffed. Neon is in the midst of a busy fall, with the indie studio releasing awards contenders such as “All of a Sudden,” “Fjord,” “Paper Tiger,” and “Artificial,” so it makes sense that it would opt to have “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” come out in the spring.

“Bad Lieutenant” first entered the cinematic vernacular with Abel Ferrara’s 1992 crime thriller that was so boundary-pushing (a nun is raped) it received an NC-17 rating. It also offered up Harvey Keitel at his most unhinged and committed, playing a cop who broke really, really bad. Then Werner Herzog transported the depravity to the Big Easy with 2009’s “Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans,” featuring Nicolas Cage at his most gonzo. Thus, an unlikely franchise was born.

The latest “Bad Lieutenant” is a U.S.-Japan co-production, produced by the late Jeremy Thomas for Recorded Picture Company, Sam Pressman for Pressman Film, Naoaki Kitajima for Nippon TV, and Misako Saka for OLM.

#3381. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

#3380. 10 Years Later, Solo Leveling Officially Admits It No Longer Needs Jinwoo

Merlyn De Souza is a freelance writer and anime enthusiast based in Goa, India, with a Bachelor's in English Literature. When she isn't writing, she can be found exploring various realms of entertainment, including, but not limited to, K-dramas, novels, and even the occasional manhwa. She also enjoys all things creative, like sewing and makeup.

To many, Sung Jinwoo has only recently been propelled into a major shonen hero with the release of Solo Leveling's anime. However, in reality, Jinwoo has been around for well over a decade at this point, with Solo Leveling's web novel serving as the blueprint for an entire sub-genre of game-like power fantasy web novels and manhwa since its release in 2016.

As far as manhwa heroes go, Jinwoo has certainly become an iconic figure and even today serves as the action fantasy genre's poster boy. That said, this hasn't stopped him from being replaced in his own sequel, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok, where Jinwoo's own son, Sung Suho, has been commanding the spotlight for the last two years straight. Admittedly, Suho has even been hailed as a better protagonist than Jinwoo, but as of late, someone else entirely has stolen the title as Jinwoo's perfect replacement.

Chapter #74 of Solo Leveling: Ragnarok has officially cemented Cha Hae-in as Jinwoo's replacement in the series with a very exciting gear update. While Jinwoo has been off in outer space keeping the Itarim at bay, Earth has been completely at the mercy of the S-rank hunters and a still-growing Sung Suho against the Itarim's Apostle and magic beasts. Solo Leveling: Ragnarok's latest arc even sees humanity pitted against another dangerous S-rank gate on par with the one on Jeju Island. But this time it seems like Cha Hae-in will be leading the charge as Solo Leveling's new solo carry in place of Jinwoo.

Solo Leveling's Jeju Island Arc is the most beloved arc in the manhwa and its one glaring plot hole has just been addressed by the series' creator.

Just when it seemed like Hae-in, Thomas Andre, and the rest of the Korean S-rank hunters had defeated the dungeon boss in Chapter #73, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok's newest chapter proves that simply breaking Sillad's spear was not the end of it. Instead, Chapter #74 of Ragnarok sees the entity animating the spear take on an even more terrifying form, using the other S-rank hunters as a source of mana after devouring them.

Suho and Hae-in are left to face the boss alone, but luckily, Beru reveals a gift hidden in the necklace Jinwoo gifted Hae-in on their wedding anniversary. The necklace is revealed to contain the Demon King's Longsword, which once belonged to Baran, the Monarch of White Flames, and came into Jinwoo's possession after he cleared the Demon Castle. This iconic lightning-sheathed sword is now in Cha Hae-in's possession, giving her a huge boost in power, and Chapter #74 of Ragnarok sees her ready to carry the entire raid armed with it.

All in all, while their victory in Chapter #73 was short-lived, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok does finally give the Korean S-rank hunters a satisfying redemption after their crushing defeat at Jeju. One of the most common criticisms of Solo Leveling over the years is that the series never really did much with its supporting cast, including its very interesting S-rank hunters who were quickly power-crept out of relevance in the final arcs.

However, the sequel has been working to fix this. Instead of a lone wolf like Jinwoo, Sung Suho has been built up as more of a team leader who has been going around collecting allies since the start of the series. Even the latest arc saw Suho give the Korean S-rank hunters a much-needed power-up with his shadow gear creations. And although they were only fighting a replica or specter of Sillad, their newest opponent was the boss of an S-rank dungeon at the end of the day, recreating the Jeju Island Arc in spirit.

But this time, instead of being utterly crushed, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok saw the S-rank hunters stand their own ground with pride — a change which even Cha Hae-in noticed. This redemption was deeply personal in its own way for every one of the Korean S-rank hunters involved. Baek Yoonho watched his closest friend die in front of him; Ma Dong-wook was killed and devoured by the Ant King; Cha Hae-in was left on death's doorstep, and Choi Jong-in was unable to protect either of them.

They were all forced to confront their powerlessness, and Solo Leveling: Ragnarok lays out this narrative and redemption beautifully, short-lived as it may have been. And now, much like Jinwoo swooped in to save the day back then, Cha Hae-in is poised to take up that role in the present, with Suho to support her along.

Solo Leveling follows Sung Jin-woo, the world's weakest hunter, who gains extraordinary powers through a mysterious program after surviving a brutal monster attack. As he navigates his newfound abilities, Jinwoo embarks on a quest to uncover the secrets of his powers and the dungeon that altered his fate.

I like 'Blade Runner 2099.' I wish I loved it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The TV gods are clearly smiling on me. Last year my favorite sci-fi series of all time, “Alien,” was adapted for TV in Hulu’s “Alien: Earth,” and now my second-favorite sci-fi series gets its own small-screen show in the form of Prime Video’s “Blade Runner 2099.”

The good news is that “Blade Runner’s” first TV show doesn’t besmirch the franchise’s good name. However, “2099” doesn’t quite manage to live up to the peerless legacy of the 1982 classic and the criminally overlooked 2017 sequel, “Blade Runner 2049.” In fact, frustration was the feeling I felt most keenly while watching the show’s first four episodes (of eight total).

Not because “Blade Runner 2099” is bad; I want to make it clear upfront this is a solid show, but because, to borrow a phrase from another iconic sci-fi universe, “We were on the verge of greatness. We were this close.” This Prime Video original gets so much right that the key areas where it comes up short stick out even more and leave me frustrated with what could have been.

Set 50 years after Ryan Gosling’s Officer K went on the hunt for Harrison Ford’s Rick Deckard, “Blade Runner 2099” leaps forward to a point in the timeline where humanity and replicants have reserved roles. The androids are on top, with humans now treated as second-class citizens, and replicant Blade Runners soon squash any fleeting thoughts of rebellion.

While it’s not the most inspired route to take — a role reversal is hardly an original narrative trope — it does set the stakes appropriately, assuming you as a viewer are rooting for the human race to prevail. Though the moral greyness of the “Blade Runner” series is here, and many replicant characters point out that they’re only doing to humanity what was done to them.

Our leads are Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant Blade Runner just days from retirement (aka impending death), and Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human resistant to the new world order, pretending to be a Replicant to secure a future for herself and her younger brother. The two soon partner up, forming less of a playful “buddy cop” dynamic and more of an icy, uneasy alliance.

There is intrigue in watching Cora try to remain undetected and in Olwen’s personal plight, as she grapples with her own morality, but despite committed work from Yeoh and Schafer, the overarching narrative threads only threaten to become truly interesting, at least at the midway point. It’s a MacGuffin hunt where the MacGuffin feels barely worth all the trouble.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Even when the narrative sputters and gets lost in meandering side quests, at least “Blade Runner 2099” consistently looks phenomenal. The grimy cyberpunk aesthetic of its sci-fi world has been successfully retained in the move from the big screen to at-home streaming. Visually, it hits all the right notes, and the foreboding score adds to the dark noir atmosphere.

But take my advice, and watch with subtitles; the dialogue audio often fades into the larger soundscape. “Blade Runner 2099” might be the first time in years I’ve had to rewind scenes multiple times just to try and decipher what the characters are actually saying to each other.

When it comes to production craft, “Blade Runner” is a triumph; it looks absolutely excellent, and sounds great too (well, apart from the dialogue levels). On the surface, it’s every bit the continuation of the “Blade Runner” universe, and as a longtime fan, that was enough to get me invested.

Where “2099” struggles is delivering enough narrative momentum to satisfy. Frustratingly early on, large chunks of the episode are a real slog, but to the show’s credit, it’s kept me coming back with well-timed narrative wrinkles. Just when my attention begins to wane, it delivers a precious, spectacular moment when it all comes together, and the clear potential is evident.

It’s these highs that will keep me watching, and as I move into the back half of the season, I hope the show’s sharpens up and fully realizes its potential. But if I were being truthful, I could see the slow pacing of the early episodes turning more than a few viewers away. “Blade Runner 2099” is in no rush. It asks viewers to be content exploring this fractured world at a crawl.

So, “Blade Runner 2099” isn’t perfect, but the franchise has always ruminated on the flaws of humanity passed down to our own android creations. Maybe the show’s unevenness could be considered poetic. Or maybe I’m just making excuses for a show I want to love more than I do.

Watch "Blade Runner 2099" on Prime Video now

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale."

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

#3377. Nathan Fillion’s ‘The Rookie’ Officially Returns With a Major Schedule Change

Since its 2018 premiere, ABC's hit procedural The Rookie has performed well for the network. The series, led by Nathan Fillion, was an immediate hit, thanks to its premise of new beginnings and personal reinvention, no matter the challenges along the way. The story started as an exploration of John Nolan, the oldest rookie in the LAPD, but has evolved into one about a sharp police officer keeping the city safe alongside his coworkers in Los Angeles' Mid-Wilshire Police Department. Eight seasons have aired so far, with a ninth set for January 2027. It will also be accompanied by a brand-new spin-off.

This is not the first time ABC has tried to expand The Rookie, with the first attempt coming in 2022 when The Rookie: Feds premiered. Headlined by Niecy Nash-Betts as Simone Clark, the FBI-set spin-off followed a similar premise: Simone leaves her career in guidance and counseling to become the FBI's oldest rookie. The Rookie: Feds ran for one season and was canceled for several reasons, including the 2023 Hollywood strikes. Some of the show's stars have continued to appear in later seasons of The Rookie.

Next year finds the mothership on the move as ABC creates The Rookie Wednesdays. Beginning January 6, 2027, The Rookie will air from 9 pm ET, followed by the new spin-off The Rookie North at 10 pm. It will be an interesting night for ratings, since NBC's juggernaut One Chicago also airs that night from 8 to 11 pm ET. CBS won't be much of a competition, since it doesn't have scripted shows that night.

The Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

You are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You said what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

ABC has already released teaser trailers for the upcoming seasons of both shows, and in The Rookie Season 9, Lucy Chen (Melissa O'Neil) and Tim Bradford (Eric Winter) are in trouble after being kidnapped during Tim's proposal. The department jumps into action to save them while they try to save themselves. Meanwhile, a new beginning takes place at 10 pm with The Rookie North. The series introduces Jay Ellis' Alex Holland, whose midlife crisis is activated by a violent home invasion. He joins the Pierce County Police Department. Rather than a slight refresh of The Rookie, the spin-off aims for a different feel by leaving the city for a slower, rural environment. The Rookie North also stars Janet Montgomery (New Amsterdam), Karen Fukuhara (The Boys), Chris Sullivan (This Is Us), Froy Gutierrez (Teen Wolf), Mya Lowe (My Life with the Walter Boys), and Malik Watson.

#3376. Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

It should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to the filmmaker’s own 2019 Oscar-winning hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has always been billed as a spinoff following the continuing adventures of his fictitious (yet still iconic) stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). But Tarantino has always loved building out his own shared and connected universe(s), and fans sure love exploring its outer limits.

“Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Manson Family, of course, and all that entails). Related Stories ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

That bent continues in “Cliff Booth,” which is rife with both out-there elements and very real references (time for that “Hee Haw” resurgence, we guess). But the film also has to follow its own series logic, which means, yes, it’s the Cliff Booth show, but hey, where are our “Hollywood” co-stars Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie)?

[Once again: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

When we first meet Cliff and Rick, the duo are long-time colleagues and best pals. As his stunt double, Cliff is tasked with doing some serious heavy lifting for Hollywood star Rick, which inevitably (?) leads them to off four members of the Manson Family. The raucous and wild violence the duo inflicts on the foursome isn’t just a fun bonding exercise for the pair. It also ensures that the nefarious group can’t go next door to enact the infamous (and very real) Tate murders. Win-win!

The film ends with an invitation for Rick to slide on over to the Tate house for a thank-you drink, presumably putting him in the path of Roman Polanski, Sharon, and all the star power they carry. “Cliff Booth” is set eight years after those events, and while Rick may have enjoyed a career upswing in the interim, his current professional endeavors have taken him far from Hollywood.

While we never see Rick in the film (despite ongoing rumors that DiCaprio might appear for a quick cameo), Cliff mentions him frequently and fondly, including telling potential paramour Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) that their professional entanglements ended when Rick got, ahem, “too fat” for Cliff to believably double him and then moved to Australia to star in the TV series “Dingo Dan.” Further details on the show are slim, but we do know it’s a Western TV show that’s proven quite popular and durable (Aussie Karen seems to like it), and Cliff makes it sound like Rick is enjoying himself. Not too bad.

By blending his two movie universes with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Tarantino got to both delight in late-’60s Hollywood magic and “save” Sharon Tate, her unborn son, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, Steven Parent, and Jay Sebring. That sort of revisionist history was the film’s buzziest twist and, as I argued at the time, the most emotional choice Tarantino has ever made in his filmography.

And while we don’t get treated to much more Sharon in “Cliff Booth,” we are granted some, in the form of a Red Apple Cigarettes commercial led by a beaming Margot Robbie, returning to her original role as the doomed actress. (The fake cigarettes are another Tarantino-verse staple, and Rick even appears in his own commercial for them during the end credits of “Hollywood.”)

In the short cameo, Sharon looks healthy and happy, and she’s clearly still enough of a star to warrant her own advertising campaign, built on her smile and her zippy shimmy. As Cliff watches the commercial at the Marina del Rey condo he shares with his dad (Peter Weller), he takes the time to stop, observe, and notably smile at the star. It’s a small grace note, and a very effective one.

One other star of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is missing from “Cliff Booth,” though. Just where the heck is Brandy?

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3372. Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’

“The Right Stuff” was released 43 years ago, but its spectacular aerial and outer space sequences have lost none of their power. Director Philip Kaufman’s adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s book, which traced the history of the test pilots who became the first astronauts, features immersive set pieces that are still as convincing as ever, in spite of decades of technological advancements since it was made. To revisit it via Criterion‘s new 4K UHD physical media release is to experience one of the most groundbreaking and enduring films of all time.

The new Criterion transfer was supervised by cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, who was still relatively early in his career when Kaufman tapped him to shoot “The Right Stuff.” Deschanel didn’t have many feature credits, but the ones he did have were impressive: his early work included the stunning imagery of “The Black Stallion” and two Hal Ashby movies, “Being There” and the Rolling Stones concert film “Let’s Spend the Night Together.” He would earn the first of his six Academy Award nominations for “The Right Stuff.” Related Stories Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March

Deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock shows at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire. Deschanel visited the set of “Minnesota” and stayed in touch with Kaufman, who called him around 10 years later with the offer to shoot “The Right Stuff.”

“It was a dream come true,” Deschanel said, noting that he had always been an aviation buff who loved going to air shows with his father. He also remembered that Kaufman wasn’t the only person on “The Right Stuff” who he had met years earlier. “Years before we had moved into our first house and needed some painting done, and we had a friend who was teaching in the Cal Arts theater department. He said, ‘I have this actor who’s really great who paints houses in the summer.'”

Deschanel hired the young actor and got to know him a little bit, and five years later was having lunch with his wife Mary Jo and Kaufman when Kaufman showed them a picture of the actor he had chosen to play John Glenn. “I said, ‘We know him. That’s Ed Harris. He painted our house,'” Deschanel said. “Then, coincidentally, the woman who was supposed to play Annie Glenn dropped out of and Phil cast my wife, so they ended up playing husband and wife in the movie.”

One of the great technical challenges of “The Right Stuff” was integrating archival footage of the space race with the new material being shot — one of the reasons the movie was shot in a 1.85:1 aspect ratio instead of a wider Panavision format as one might have expected for such an epic film. “We were using actual footage of NASA’s rocket launches and things like that, and they were filming in the old-fashioned 4:3 format using the full frame of a 35mm camera,” Deschanel said. “Converting that to widescreen was really impossible.”

Working in close collaboration with visual effects supervisor Gary Gutierrez (who provides a fascinating look at the film’s miniature and rear-projection work on the Criterion disc), Deschanel solved the numerous logistical problems that came with trying to make it look as though the actors were hurtling through the air at the speed of sound and beyond. Even when Gutierrez thought he had solutions that would work, they often had to be tweaked to accommodate Kaufman’s desire to make everything feel as realistic and immersive as possible.

Early attempts to use a motion-control system for the effects, for example, were discarded because the camera movement was too smooth for Kaufman’s purposes. “Phil wanted it to have some energy to it,” Deschanel said. “That changed the whole methodology.” Whenever rockets were taking off or various crafts were flying, Deschanel made sure to add some shake to the camera. “I actually gave my camera operator, Craig Denault, a black eye at one point because I was hitting the camera so hard.”

In addition to the expected challenges, there were plenty of unexpected ones as well — like the fact that Sam Shepard, who played ace pilot Chuck Yeager, wouldn’t fly. “The only time he ever went up in an airplane was when Yeager took him for a flight,” Deschanel said. “Other than that, whenever we had a mockup of an X-1 or the F-104 or anything like that, he’d make me get in and show him how it was going to twist and turn before he would get into it.” For Yeager’s scenes and many of the others, rear projection was used — meaning Deschanel had to photograph what was seen outside the pilots’ and astronauts’ windows long before the actors’ material was actually shot.

“There was a lot of complexity to all those things,” Deschanel said. “But it gave it a real energy and sense of being there. And that’s what you try to discover as you’re filming any film: what is that visual metaphor that really makes you believe you’re having the same experience the characters are having?” Creating that sense of authenticity required some unorthodox approaches, as when Deschanel had a Learjet pilot take the nose cone off of his plane and replace it with a clear dome.

“We put a camera in there with a 15mm lens, and then we were able to go up above 50,000 feet,” Deschanel said. “At that level, it’s so dark, it’s almost like you’re in outer space. Anything you could think of to find the reality of the movie, we employed.” Deschanel’s perfectionism became the stuff of legend over the years, with some people who worked on “The Right Stuff” claiming he insisted on shooting only at sunrise or sunset to get the most beautiful possible images — a myth Deschanel is quick to dispel.

“The fact is we shot all day long and had really long days,” Deschanel said. “There was one point where, just to finish up at Edwards Air Force Base, I was on for 24 hours and changed the crew in the middle. So I had a whole new crew for the second half of that long day.” That said, Deschanel acknowledges that the film’s justly famous exteriors were important to him, in part for what they represented.

“The iconic moment is when Yeager is on horseback, and he rides up and sees the X-1,” Deschanel said. “It’s like ‘The Professionals’ or ‘The Wild Bunch,’ these movies about the end of the West as new technology takes over. To me, there’s this wonderful representation of the end of an era when Yeager comes across this fighter jet. Then, of course, he flies it and breaks the sound barrier. So it’s this wonderful juxtaposition of important moments in human history, where one person does something that further advances flight to the point that makes it possible for the next generation to go into outer space. I always miss that I never got to make a Western, but in a way, ‘The Right Stuff’ is a Western.”

“The Right Stuff” special edition 4K UHD release is now available from Criterion.

#3371. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

#3370. 7 'Peanuts' Episodes That Are 10/10 Animated Masterpieces, Ranked

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Peanuts has outlasted almost every cartoon on television, and its holiday specials are its bread and butter. Thanksgiving is Thursday, and A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving is streaming only on Apple TV this year, with no traditional linear broadcast airing. However, a new special, Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, premiered on November 13th, featuring songs from Laufey and John Legend.

Together, the entire library makes the holiday season a perfect time to rank the specials that have built so many family traditions. A note on the choices. I picked specials that critics and viewers both live on and that tie to a date on the calendar. Streaming windows can be quick to change, so check Apple TV before you queue anything up. Spoilers, of course, are not a concern for specials this familiar in the public conversation.

Happy New Year, Charlie Brown! starts on the last day of school before Christmas break, when Charlie Brown's teacher assigns a book report on Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace. Charlie Brown ends up dreading his entire vacation, and attempts every shortcut imaginable around reading the novel. He asks a store whether it comes in a variety of different creative forms, including a computer game. Peppermint Patty keeps calling to invite him to her party, and Marcie, Sally, and Lucie get swept up in the drama of it all.

Charlie brings War and Peace to the party and tries to read it on the porch, but he falls asleep and misses the midnight countdown. The Little Red-Haired Girl shows up and ends up dancing with Linus. But by the end, Charlie finally finishes the book and turns in his report. The special is also a small musical, with songs by Ed Bogas and Desireé Goyette, including a dance lesson number. IMDb users rate the special 7.2, and Collider ranks it third among its best Peanuts specials.

Peppermint Patty spends nearly her entire allowance on eggs in It's the Easter Beagle, Charlie Brown! It is mainly due to the fact Marcie keeps ruining the eggs after she tries to show her how to dye them. She fries the first batch on a griddle, then cracks the next batch before boiling it. Meanwhile, Snoopy tries to find Woodstock a new home and botches that through several different birdhouse attempts. Linus swears the Easter Beagle will hand out eggs, yet Sally doubts him after the Great Pumpkin fiasco.

On Easter morning, Snoopy turns out to be the Easter Beagle. He distributes eggs, including one for Lucy, but runs out before reaching Charlie Brown. The special earned an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Children's Special, and CBS aired it every Easter from 1974 till 2000. Peppermint Patty's exasperated shouts became a running gag moment. IMDb users rate it at 7.5. Its plot is a little thin, but the visual gags, such as Snoopy's dance in a department store, foster memorable moments. Todd Barbee voiced Charlie Brown for the final time, and Linda Ercoli played Peppermint Patty.

The Peanuts are still doing Christmas like no one else can.

Charlie Brown incessantly checks his mailbox over and over in Be My Valentine, convinced that one is on the way. Like the Easter Beagle episode, this one aired on CBS for 25 years. At school, Charlie arrives with a briefcase to carry all the cards and love he expects to get. Snoopy builds an elaborate music box valentine and stages a puppet show about love. Linus, has a massive crush on his teacher, Miss Othmar. He buys her a huge box of chocolates before learning later on she has left with her boyfriend.

Sally mistakes the gift for her own and makes Linus a valentine in return. Unfortunately for Charlie yet again, he ends the day with a single candy heart that reads, "Forget it, kid." Linus chucks the chocolates he got off a bridge, where Snoopy and Woodstock are positioned to catch and eat them. After the special first aired, children across the country sent valentines to Charlie Brown. Violet's used valentine and Snoopy's surprise kiss give the special a bittersweet ending. A follow-up, A Charlie Brown Valentine, was released in 2002, and IMDb users rated the original 7.3.

Charlie Brown's All-Stars! was the first Peanuts special not constructed around a holiday. After Charlie Brown's baseball team quits on him after another loss, he finds himself at his lowest. The hardware store owner, Mr. Hennessy, offers to sponsor the team, put them in an organized league, and buy them real uniforms. The kids rush back, but Charlie Brown soon realizes that the league does not allow girls or dogs. He's then forced to choose between the new gear, and his loyalty to Lucy, Violet, Patty, Frieda, and Snoopy.

Charlie turns down the offer and keeps the secret until after the game. It, of course, leaves his team enraged after they lose. Schroeder finally scolds the girls for their selfishness, and they make Charlie Brown a uniform from Linus's blanket. Yahoo ranks the special fifth among the Peanuts episodes, and IMDb users rate it at 7.5. A Record Store Day release with music from the special is scheduled for November 27th, and the uniform storyline returned in a 1996 remake. The moral decision gives Charlie Brown one of his most admirable moments.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving premiered on CBS on November 20th, 1973. It begins when Peppermint Patty invites herself and her friends over to Charlie Brown's for dinner. Charlie is forced to improvise a meal. Snoopy, Woodstock, and Linus help him prepare a feast of toast, pan-fried popcorn, pretzel sticks, jelly beans, and sundaes. Patty rejects the meal for lacking traditional values and foods, until Marcie reminds her that she invited herself.

Rotten Tomatoes lists A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving at 67% from critics and 76% from audiences, a modest score for a special that families consistently rewatch every year. Linus tells the story of the first Thanksgiving along the way, while Snoopy and Woodstock's more traditional meal back at the doghouse adds a touch of sweetness. Peppermint Patty later asks Marcie to apologize for her, an echo of The Courtship of Miles Standish, and then apologizes directly.

In It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, Linus keeps a lonely vigil in a pumpkin patch, certain that the Great Pumpkin will rise. Apple describes the special as Charlie Brown prepping for a party, Snoopy setting his sights on the Red Baron, and Linus awaiting a miracle. Sally joins Linus and misses the party, which leads to one of the funniest rants in the series. Snoopy's Flying Ace sequence turns a doghouse into a World War I airplane.

The special marked its 60th anniversary this year, which ends with Charlie Brown returning home from trick or treating with a bag of rocks. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 90% from critics and 85% from audiences. Yahoo's ranking of the Peanuts specials put it first and calls it the best Halloween cartoon ever. After it aired, children across the nation sent candy to Charlie Brown and Vince Guaraldi's score includes The Great Pumpkin Waltz.

A Charlie Brown Christmas opens with Charlie feeling down and depressed about the commercialism of the holiday. Charles M. Schulz wrote it, Bill Melendez directed, and Lee Mendelsohn produced. It aired on CBS every year from 1965 till 2000, and then through ABC until 2019. Lucy asks Charlie to direct the gang's Christmas play, and he buys a small, scrawny tree that his friends end up mocking. The special used real child voice actors and left out a laugh track. These were choices that worried CBS mightily at the time, before it won an Emmy and a Peabody Award.

Snoopy decorates his doghouse for a contest, and Linus calmly recites the Christmas story from the Gospel of Luke. Vince Guaraldi's jazz score, including Linus and Lucy and Christmastime Is Here, became as famous as the special itself. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 86% from critics and 93% from audiences. The 61st anniversary falls on December 9th.

#3369. Scarlett Johansson’s New Horror Reboot Officially Continues 53-Year Rating Streak

Scarlett Johansson's The Exorcist: Martyrs will be pulling no punches.

Johansson is teaming up with Mike Flanagan for the latest reboot of the classic horror franchise, starring as New York City homicide detective Julie Miller as she is pulled into a dark murder investigation with apparent ties to a former Satanic serial killer she helped stop. Also starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Diane Lane, Jacobi Jupe and Sasha Lane, among many others, The Exorcist: Martyrs is currently on track for a March 12 release date.

Now, with just over two months until it hits theaters, the Motion Picture Association has officially given The Exorcist: Martyrs an R rating, continuing the horror franchise's 53-year streak of landing the mature rating. The site further explains that the new reboot's rating stems from its "bloody violent content, grisly images, language, and some sexual references."

In addition to the franchise's tradition, The Exorcist: Martyrs securing an R-rating also continues Flanagan's streak of more mature films in the director's chair. Across his eight released films, only two have landed a PG-13 rating from the MPA, those being Netflix's Before I Wake and Blumhouse's Ouija: Origin of Evil. His TV shows have similarly landed firmly in the TV-MA rating, generally stemming from explicit language and, in recent years, some bloodier set pieces.

Interestingly, while it keeps the series' 53-year streak alive, The Exorcist: Martyr's R-rating does immediately stand out from its predecessors with its promise of "grisly images." Though the horror franchise is well-known for its more visceral material, the only other movie to explicitly list its gruesome imagery as part of its R-rating was that of the infamous Exorcist: The Beginning prequel film. See the chart below for the full franchise list of ratings and given reasons from the MPA:

Strong violence and gore, disturbing images and rituals, and for language including some sexual dialogue.

Some violent content, disturbing images, language and sexual references.

Bloody violent content, grisly images, language, and some sexual references.

The first Exorcist: Martyrs trailer already showcased Flanagan leaning into more gruesome territory for his reboot of the classic horror series. The crime scenes Johansson's character inspects come complete with dead bodies mutilated in different ritualistic manners, while another sequence saw Julie inspecting a barrel later with an unknown entity emerging and coated in blood. As Flanagan himself teased to ScreenRant, he was not looking to pull any punches with his film, calling it "very, very bloody":

Mike Flanagan: Yeah, I think the only thing that comes close to the amount of blood is we did melt that orgy in The Fall of the House of Usher in acid. That was pretty bloody, but that was funny, I thought. [Chuckles] As dark as it was, this is vicious, and that isn't a muscle I get to flex very often. It's very disturbing, and that was part of the fun of it. This whole story just felt very unsafe from the beginning, and yeah, that isn't a gear I go toward frequently. I like hope and heart and humanism, and there are moments of that if you squint, but this is a dark story, and it is scary. So yeah, that was very exciting for me, too.

With Flanagan also having been largely inspired by the cult favorite Exorcist III for his take on the franchise, it will be interesting to see if The Exorcist: Martyrs finds itself leaning closer to the 1990 film's atmosphere than the visceral nature of its 2004 successor. Given early test screenings, per the director, have been glowing, as has the response to the trailer thus far, it does at least seem like this push into hard-R territory is going to give viewers an unforgettable experience.

Thirteen years after stopping a satanic serial killer, New York City detective Julie Miller confronts a new murderer who appears connected to her past. With help from a former prison chaplain and a rookie detective, she investigates a sinister connection between history's most notorious killers.
