It was 2013, and future Helix Sleep co-founders Adam Tishman, Jerry Lin and Kristian von Rickenbach had a simple mission: to find a comfy new mattress that wouldn't break the bank.

But instead of an enjoyable shopping experience, the trio were faced with confusing online cliches, or pricey mattresses from brick and mortar stores.

Quickly, an opportunity sprung up in front of them: to disrupt a tired industry and subsequently create one of America's leading sleep brands.

Fast forward to present day and Helix Sleep is making some of the best mattresses we've tested, chief among them being the Helix Midnight Luxe, which is currently 25% off at Helix.

In an exclusive interview for Tom's Guide, Helix co-founder Jerry Lin talks us through the conception, creation and rebirth of the Midnight Luxe, our top-rated mattress for side sleepers, and what the future looks like for this award-wining bed.

The Midnight Luxe is always included in the monthly Helix mattress sale, but this month's discount is higher than normal. For Black Friday you can save 25% on every size, with a queen costing $1,874 (was $2,498). You'll also get a year's sleep trial, lifetime warranty, and free shipping.

Tishman, Lin and von Rickenbach identified three big problems when trying to buy a new mattress:

The trio started working with sleep PHD researchers in Europe to design a line of mattresses that weren't one-size-fits-all, but instead distinguishable by sleep position. (And by looking closely at our sleep DNA, the brand name Helix was born.)

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

When Helix Sleep finally launched in 2015, they did so with a direct-to-consumer model. They sought to demystify the mattress buying process by creating bespoke mattresses based on your answers to the Helix Sleep quiz.

After thousands of online orders, in 2017 the brand mined the sleep quiz data to roll out a basic range of mattresses that catered to every major sleep position.

Soon after, the original Helix Midnight entered the online marketplace. Now the entry level bed in the brand's expanded range, the Core Midnight is designed to meet the needs of a typical side sleeper; cushioning at the shoulders, hips and knees, and support at the lower back.

In terms of mattress firmness, we'd rate the Core Midnight as a medium. It was a great start for improved side sleep comfort, but the best was yet to come...

In 2018, Helix Sleep launched the Luxe Collection. Maintaining its philosophy of mattresses tailored for every individual sleep need, this new and more luxurious range of beds aimed to elevate the comfort of the Core mattresses to appeal to customers seeking a truly indulgent sleep.

The original inspiration was straightforward: take the medium-feel of our original Helix Midnight and elevate it with the comfort, materials, and craftsmanship you'd expect from a luxury hotel mattress

“The Helix Luxe Collection is our most popular mattress line, with the Midnight Luxe consistently ranking as our best-selling model,” reveals Lin, a Wharton MBA who began his career in investment banking.

“The original inspiration was straightforward: take the medium-feel, side-sleeper-friendly design of our original Helix Midnight and elevate it with the comfort, materials, and craftsmanship you'd expect from a luxury hotel mattress, but at a much more accessible price point."

The timing of the 2018 launch couldn’t have been better. With original mattress-in-a-box brands Casper and Purple disrupting the traditional brick-and-mortar mattress industry, Helix and its Luxe line became an integral part of the growing boxed bed revolution.

Then, just two years later, many parts of the States found themselves under stay-at-home orders as part of Covid-19 quarantine measures.

One of Helix's biggest competitive advantages is that we manufacture our own foam

With 'work from bed' the new normal for many Americans, and with little else to spend hard-earned cash on, the e-commerce mattress industry boomed.

Some even reported that the Helix Midnight Luxe was the only thing helping them sleep during those uncertain times.

With the bed-to-door industry on fast forward, Helix wanted to keep the Midnight Luxe ahead of the curve. The answer lay in doubling down: improving the mattress from base to quilted cover.

The Midnight Luxe stands at 13.5" tall and is crafted from a combination of coils and comfort foam.

Each layer serves a specific purpose for its overall sleep comfort.

From top to bottom, let's take a closer look at the Luxe's overall structure:

A soft, breathable cover sits above two layers of premium quilting foam (1.5 lb and gel-infused 1.8 lb), creating a plush sleep surface that's both comfortable and durable. The standard cover is made with TENCEL fabric.

An additional layer of gel memory foam provides targeted pressure relief, particularly around the shoulders and hips, making the Midnight Luxe especially well-suited for side sleepers. This gel memory foam has an IFD (Indentation Force Deflection) of 10-18 and a density of 1.8-4.0 PCF.

Helix's signature titanium, graphite, and copper infused memory foam delivers deeper contouring and is engineered for temperature management and long-term durability. It has a 4lb foam density, which is more than double the 2lb density of many foams used by standard brands.

Next, A firmer transition layer, with lower density foam, creates a gradual shift from the plush comfort layers to the supportive coil system underneath. This helps prevent the sensation of sinking too deeply into the mattress.

Up to 1,000 individually wrapped eight-inch coils provide responsive support, with enhanced reinforcement in the lumbar region to help promote healthy spinal alignment. Reinforced perimeter coils also improve edge support, making the full surface of the mattress more usable. Each coil is made from tempered steel and wrapped in polypropylene non-woven fabric.

The Helix Midnight Luxe is a luxury hybrid mattress. While the coils are in important factor in the bed's overall comfort layer, it is the proprietary foams that help set this boxed bed apart from many competitors.

While most brands use pre-poured foams from third party suppliers, Helix manufacture their own foam (more on this below). This should allow them to fine tune its construction until the optimal level of comfort is achieved. A feat I think they've pulled it off.

As someone who sleeps predominantly on my side and occasionally on my back, I feel as though the Helix Midnight Luxe has been crafted specifically for me in way that I haven't experienced while testing another mattress

The foams provide just the right amount of body-contouring support across the shoulders, hips and knees, while holding the spine in healthy alignment with the rest of the body.

In 2022, Helix merged with sleep brand Brooklyn Bedding. Now operating from its own factory in Arizona, Helix began experimenting with pouring and manufacturing its own mattress foam, alongside its own coils.

This decision proved to be a pivotal moment in the development of the Midnight Luxe.

“One of Helix's biggest competitive advantages is something most consumers never see: we manufacture our own foam,” explains Lin, who built the finance and operations backbone behind Helix’s growth and helps steer the brand’s product innovation and retail expansion.

“Many mattress brands are essentially assemblers. They source foam, coils, and other components from third-party suppliers and combine them into a finished product.

“At Helix, we take a different approach. We manufacture our core components ourselves, giving us significantly more control over material quality, performance, and cost.

“A perfect example is the proprietary memory foam we developed specifically for the Luxe Collection.”

We developed a high-density, 4lb memory foam infused with titanium, graphite and copper

“For the latest Midnight Luxe, we developed a high-density, 4lb memory foam infused with titanium, graphite and copper,” explains Lin. “This is one of the most important innovations in the redesigned mattress.”

Foam density is an important factor in overall durability. Higher-density memory foams can offer greater resistance to daily use, wear and compression, helping the Midnight Luxe to maintain its comfort and support through years of use.

And with a queen costing in the region of $1,900 when not on sale, durability is crucial.

However, as someone who has tested both versions of the Helix Midnight Luxe, it's worth noting that the trade off of this durability is that the 2025 redesigned model is slightly firmer.

"At 4lb per cubic foot, this is a premium-density memory foam engineered for long-term performance," explains Lin.

For context, many luxury manufacturer's use foams under 2lb in density, with 1.8lb considered an acceptable density.

Helix also incorporates three distinct materials into the foam formulation, each selected for its specialist properties. These are:

By manufacturing its own foam, the brand can refine density, responsiveness and body-cradling characteristics until it's achieved the desired balance.

For the Midnight Luxe in particular, that means "deep pressure relief without sacrificing the support that makes the [mattress] so comfortable," says Lin.

"It's a level of material customization that would be much more difficult if we were simply purchasing off-the-shelf foam."

“While the deeper comfort layers are important, we also paid attention to the part of the mattress you feel first: the quilted pillow top,” says Lin.

"The plush pillow top is a quilted comfort system made with two layers of high-density foam, a 1.5lb layer and a 1.8lb gel-infused layer.

“These layers are designed to provide immediate cushioning and pressure relief, particularly around sensitive areas like the shoulders and hips."

While pressure relief is a crucial feature of any mattress designed specifically for side sleepers, there was another reason the brand invested in higher-density materials at the top — durability.

"The uppermost layers of a mattress experience significant daily compression and wear," explains Lin. "Using higher-quality foam in these layers helps the Midnight Luxe to maintain its comfort characteristics over time.

"By incorporating 1.5lb and 1.8lb foams, we're making a deliberate investment in materials that go beyond what's commonly used in the industry."

For context, both the Saatva Classic, the highest-scoring mattress we've ever tested, and the DreamCloud Classic, our second highest ranking mattress overall because of its superb value for money, use a foam density of 1.4lb in their Euro top covers, which are inherently different by design to the plush pillow top on the Midnight Luxe.

The Helix Midnight Luxe launched in 2018 as a luxury hotel-style upgrade to the original Midnight (now marketed as the Core Midnight). It has a plush pillow top and zoned lumbar support for back pain relief.

"Those features helped establish the Luxe Collection as our most popular mattress line," says Lin.

"But as our manufacturing capabilities evolved, we saw an opportunity to make more meaningful improvements to the mattress itself."

In 2025, Helix introduced the most significant redesign of the Luxe Collection since its launch.

Rather than focusing on cosmetic changes or additional features, they sought to reengineer the mattress from the inside out.

"These improvements reflect how we think about product development at Helix," says Lin.

"We're constantly looking for ways to improve the actual sleep experience, whether that's through better pressure relief, more consistent support, improved temperature regulation, or materials that maintain their performance longer.

"Ultimately, our philosophy is simple: a luxury mattress should be defined by the quality of what's inside it, not just how it looks or how much it costs," concludes Lin.

"That's what guided the latest Midnight Luxe redesign, and it's what continues to drive our approach to mattress innovation."

#3367. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

#3366. Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion

It’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024. But if it feels like the black and white, silent, slapstick indie comedy still hasn’t left the cultural conversation, that’s because in all that time it has continued to quietly play in theaters and attract audiences both loyal and new alike.

Technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters. It continues to play individual screenings in a city or two every weekend. Now, though, “Hundreds of Beavers” is set to return to theaters for what is its biggest theatrical expansions to date. The film will kick off its third annual Northwoods Christmas, which will feature 130 screenings across 85 cities, with more to likely be added in the coming weeks. It came about after another fan campaign pushed for the film to come to some markets it hadn’t previously thought about or targeted such as Indianapolis and Charlottesville, and it will now play in everything from concert venues to microcinemas. Related Stories Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’ Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a new Christmas movie. The first time “Hundreds of Beavers” was re-released at Christmas 2024, which was shortly after the Blu-ray for the film became available, it brought in $118K at the box office in a month, and the producers continued the tradition in 2025.

“There’s room for a Christmas tradition with the energy of a ‘Rocky Horror’ screening,” said producer Kurt Ravenwood. “You can watch ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ and ‘White Christmas’ all you want, but for getting together with friends and family to laugh about the miserable winter ahead, ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ has them all beat.”

Each of the screenings will be preceded by a short film featuring “Bing Crosbeaver,” which they did last year, but this will be a new short with a new twist in which another character named “Conspirabeaver” will be joined by a “sinister foe,” per the release. Some of the in-person beavers in costume will be present at the screenings, and fans will also get a promotional poster for the movie. The “Beavers” team recently released a few parody posters ripping off the recent releases of “You Can See Everything,” “Digger,” and “The Devils.”

To date, “Hundreds of Beavers” has made $940,092 at the domestic box office, including another $618,014 internationally to bring its worldwide total to above $1.5 million. It’s done all this via first producing the film for just $150,000 and spending little more than $70,000 on ads, publicity, and its many roadshow screenings. It’s also been released entirely independently, starting with a run in the Midwest where the film is set before it started expanding to the coasts.

Incredibly, more than 70 percent of the film’s U.S. box office has come after “Hundreds of Beavers” began streaming way back on April 15, 2024, and it has even sold more than 20,000 Blu-Rays worldwide. It’s a rare, truly indie success story even in a day and age when many movies have pursued self-distribution strategies.

For those who haven’t had the pleasure of seeing “Hundreds of Beavers” in theaters yet, the film is about a drunken applejack salesman who loses everything and has to survive the winter by becoming North America’s greatest fur trapper. It sees the trapper wrestling and fighting with dozens of beavers and other forest animals all wearing mascot suits, with the stark black and white cinematography and creative physical stunts embracing a zany video game logic and absurd silent comedy slapstick gags.

The film is directed by Mike Cheslik and was written by Cheslik and star Ryland Tews, with the film also starring Olivia Graves, Wes Tank, Doug Mancheski, and Luis Rico.

#3365. I’m a Deals Writer, and These Are My Top 10 Tech Deals This Week

As Lifehacker's deals writer, I'm always looking for the best bargains on TVs, speakers, laptops, and other tech. Now that it's Friday, I've rounded up this week's sales highlights.

This week, you can already feel the early Black Friday deals heating up with the sale starting next week. Amazon has many tech deals, as do Costco, Walmart, and other retailers. You can find price cuts on the M5 MacBook Air, the best headphones of 2026, Kindle readers, and more.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 are one of the best premium headphones of 2026, and right now, Amazon is offering them with a 24% on them right now. That brings the price of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones down to $348. You're not likely to see these headphones drop any further in price anytime soon, even with Black Friday coming up. So if you've had your eyes on the XM6, this is likely the best deal you'll get for a while.

The Kindle Paperwhite is having one of its best discounts right now, dropping to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors. This is the classic, standard e-reader from Amazon, but since it's not the Signature Edition, you'll have to put up with ads and the minimum 16GB storage (which still gets you storage for over a thousand e-books). There are other e-readers on sale as well if you want to see other options.

The MacBook Air with the M5 chip comes in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $250 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,049.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,249 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case.

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269). This is a great opportunity to snatch a quality portable speaker with a big discount.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $19.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade.

The Sony WH-CH730N are $98 (originally $179), the lowest price they've ever been. They use the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0.

Samsung’s HW-Q600F soundbar is down to $379.99 at Amazon from $499.99, a $120 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever. This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup. Dolby Atmos also brings a modest sense of height, and effects track cleanly from left to right. You get a graphic equalizer and sound presets for adjusting the audio to your preferences through the included remote.

The Ultimate Ears Miniroll is down to $49.99 (originally $79.99), the second-lowest it has sold for so far. It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. Despite its size, the Miniroll can get surprisingly loud—which PCMag confirms in its review—and at moderate volume, it has enough sound for a kitchen or backyard without sounding thin. As for its battery life, you get about 12 hours of playback before it needs a charge over USB-C, while its IP67 rating protects it from dust and a brief dunk in water.

If you're looking for a premium model, Samsung’s 65-inch S90H OLED TV is down to $1,397.99 from $2,697.99 at launch, saving you over $1,000. The sale price is easier to justify when you consider that this is a new 2026 model. If the 65-inch model does not suit your space, Samsung also sells the S90H in 42-, 48-, 55-, 77-, and 83-inch versions, and those sizes are discounted as well.

#3364. Hunter Schafer Breaks Down the Meaning Behind 'Blade Runner 2099's Final Scenes

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for the entire season of Blade Runner 2099.Blade Runner 2099 is officially out — the thrilling eight-episode series from creator/showrunner Silka Luisa drops today on Prime Video. The series takes place 50 years after Blade Runner 2049 and 90 years after the Ridley Scott film. 2099 introduces us to a version of Los Angeles we've never seen before — one run by replicants. We meet Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human working undercover as a replicant Blade Runner. Hiding in plain sight, Cora slowly learns the truth behind this replicant-run world while partnered with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who is dying within a matter of days.

The series takes Cora and Olwen across Los Angeles, ultimately leading them to discover that what they're hunting for is the truth of the Nexus-1 replicants. Cora learns that her adoptive mother, Helena (Sheila Atim) was one of the original replicants, born alongside Julius (Tom Burke), who eventually killed her while hunting for Tyrell's memory, which hold the secret to creating more Nexus-1 replicants. The series ends ambiguously, with Cora returning to the LAPD after Julius' death and Olwen journeying off to space, uncertain whether she's set to discover new worlds or simply finish off the last remaining days of her life.

Collider spoke with both Schafer and Yeoh about that surprising Blade Runner 2099 finale. The two actors discuss their characters' changing relationships and what leads Cora to protecting Olwen in that final fight against Julius. Yeoh also breaks down that thrilling fight with Clotilde (Amy Lennox) and why that scene was so important for Olwen. Schafer contemplates Cora's final conversation with Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), and what it might mean for the two humans caught in a world full of replicants.

COLLIDER: One of the scenes I really liked in the finale is seeing Cora protecting Olwen from Julius; I thought that was such a great scene to show the development of their relationship. Can you guys talk about developing that bond between these two characters and going from enemies to these close friends?

HUNTER SCHAFER: Yeah. I mean, it was so magical, as we were getting to know each other as we were getting to know our own respective characters better throughout the filming process; it sort of coincided with the growth of Cora and Olwen's relationship. I think it was a matter of exploring it; I think moments would reveal themselves as more human or intimate with us, depending on the nature of the scene. But I really loved... I mean, especially by Episode 6 when they're really seeing each other for who they are; from then there's a beauty to the mutual understanding.

MICHELLE YEOH: I think the most important thing is that there were no more secrets. Because at the beginning, she had her secrets. She was like a bloody human trying to pretend to be a replicant! That's horrifying for Olwen, who is the replicant who thinks she knows everything and knows what it takes to be a replicant and to be lied to by someone like that.

But, at that point, when we came to confront each other and then finally understand that we both had secrets that we kept from each other, and that secrets freed us and made our bond stronger and made us work together, because we were on the same mission, right? We needed to find what was the answer that could destroy this very fragile place that we have. So I think it was important as a human and as a replicant, we have to work together; otherwise, everything will go to hell.

Along the way, they have learned in very strange ways to care for each other, and that bond was beautiful, because, right at the end, it was like, we fought for each other, not just with each other, but at the end it was how to defend ourselves. So I don't think Cora at any point would not jump in front if she felt Olwen was in trouble.

SCHAFER: Yeah, there's a real kinship by the end.

Michelle, you have this great scene where Olwen's fighting Clotilde, and she has the chance to let her fall to her death. Why do you think that she takes that moment and saves her? Because, obviously, that comes in to benefit her later on, but, at that moment, she could just let her die.

YEOH: I know, I think this is almost like a flashback to Roy Batty and Deckard at that point, where it's like, what is humanity? Does it mean that if you were born as a replicant, you can't find the humanity, you don't understand it? And, at that point, you're right, Olwen could have let her go, because she was getting so badly beaten up by Clotilde. I mean, she could have just [been] like, "Die, you bitch," you know? [Laughs] And then I can just move on to do other things. But then that's what it takes to be human. To save another, whether it's someone who doesn't have a soul or has a soul or whatever it is, but not to just let someone die. And I think that was the humanity that suddenly struck Olwen, and she didn't let go, which then also transferred to Clotilde, because otherwise she would not have had clarity in her head.

SCHAFER: Yeah, they both had desires to live.

YEOH: Yes, and also desires to know the truth. Like, what is this guy Julius selling us? Because he's the one that's like, "I gave you this. This is what you could have. You would come back, and you'd be stronger, and you wouldn't have to die." It was a very special moment in that scene which just turned things around.

Hunter, for you, Cora has that final scene with Greta, and I think it's just such an intriguing moment, especially since I really love Greta in the show. What's your read on what's happening there between these two people?

SCHAFER: I think Blade Runner is famous for its open-ended conclusions in that they are open to interpretation, but I think Cora sees herself in Greta. And Greta is such an intriguing character, in another way, I think, as a human who has infiltrated the LAPD in that world of Blade Runners. Greta is a human as well. So, I think there's a kinship that she feels there, even though they've barely spoken. They've only really done a few empathy tests together and had a few interactions, but human-to-human, there still is that connection together.

YEOH: Yeah, that poor human was actually quite a sad figure because she's forced to be there because she has a gift of being able to detect. And I think she detected that in Cora at the beginning because she sort of reached out to call for help, like help me get away from this.

SCHAFER: Well, yeah, I love that because you're not just part of the test, or if it's really her.

YEOH: Yeah, exactly! And that was like, whoa! Is Cora going to "fall for it"? Is it real? That was so cool.

SCHAFER: And then she drops her face, and Cora passes the test; it's awesome.

#3363. Casting HBO's Baldur's Gate Series: All 10 BG3 Party Members

Streaming platforms are in full swing with live-action video game adaptations, and HBO’s upcoming Baldur’s Gate series is among the most exciting currently in development. Reportedly set after the events of Baldur’s Gate 3, the show looks set to bring one of the most iconic settings from Dungeons & Dragons to the small screen. The city of Baldur’s Gate offers enormous possibilities for a live-action D&D TV show, especially since it follows on from the events of the hugely popular video game series.

Details remain scarce, but for fans of Baldur’s Gate 3, a key question is who will play its beloved characters if they return. Many want original performers such as Neil Newbon and Jennifer English to reprise their roles, and the HBO show’s developer, The Last Of Us’s Craig Mazin, has expressed interest in involving the game’s cast (via Deadline). However, his enthusiasm doesn’t guarantee that they’ll definitely return, or that they’ll play the same characters. Fortunately, there are some more than suitable actors to fill the shoes of any familiar party members returning in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series.

Astarion can make an appalling suggestion sound like the most entertaining idea in the room. He has a unique combination of elegance, malice, and impeccable comic timing, all of which is familiar territory for Tom Hiddleston, whose performance as Loki made the MCU’s trickster god’s wounded pride and theatrical mischief irresistible. He’s also got prior experience playing a vampire thanks to 2013’s Only Lovers Left Alive. Both roles capture something that’s essential to Astarion: the arrogance of immortality being used to mask a sense of desperation and need for a greater purpose than simply living forever.

Tom Hiddleston could deliver Astarion’s most withering remarks with ease while also making the sudden disappearance of that confidence feel just as unsettling in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate TV show as it was in BG3. Any actor playing Astarion requires an understanding of how a charming character can quickly become a terrifying one. Hiddleston has the skills to make Astarion hilarity land without him being reduced to comic relief. He could make BG3’s vampire rogue funny, unsettling, and emotionally complex, all of which would be essential when following in the footsteps of Neil Newbon’s performance in the game.

Ben Barnes has already shown how fun to watch a charming, articulate man with dangerous magical ambitions can be. His time as General Kirigan/The Darkling in Netflix’s Shadow and Bone is a great glimpse of how he might handle Gale’s susceptibility to power in a live-action Baldur’s Gate story, while The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian demonstrates the sincerity needed for the wizard’s more approachable side. Any actor playing Gale needs to balance both sides for the performance to land.

The greatest challenge if Gale makes an appearance in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series is ensuring the Wizard of Waterdeep feels approachable despite his intellectual ego. His elaborate explanations and social awkwardness make him considerably warmer than a stereotypical mysterious fantasy sorcerer. Still, this should never mean he comes across as weak or incapable. Roles like Billy Russo in The Punisher prove that Ben Barnes has no issue portraying characters who are charming yet still dangerous, especially those driven by ambitions those around them would struggle to understand.

Karlach should look capable of throwing an enemy across a room without breaking a sweat, and WWE superstar Rhea Ripley would make that immediately believable. While not an experienced actor, her wrestling career supplies the strength, explosive movement, and physical confidence needed for a tiefling barbarian who has survived the Blood War. Just as important is her ability to command attention through posture and facial expressions. Ripley can make a grin feel like a challenge or an invitation, a promising quality for a character whose excitement about being alive is just as memorable as her capacity for destruction.

True, it would be an ambitious move into dramatic acting for Rhea Ripley, especially given how much pain sits beneath Karlach’s enthusiasm. Her infernal engine makes the simple possibility of touching someone devastatingly important, and those scenes demand tenderness as much as rage. Ripley’s suitability for the role lies in the combination of playfulness with being physically intimidating. If she can pull of the more nuanced side of Karlach’s character too, she’ll be more than ideal for HBO’s Baldur’s Gate TV show cast.

Anya Taylor-Joy’s work as the titular road warrior in Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga makes a solid argument for giving her a sword and very little patience in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series. Characters like Furiosa as well as Margot in The Menu are all the evidence needed that she can communicate determination through a fixed stare and a stubborn refusal to show weakness, which is essential for Lae’zel. The Githyanki fighter’s severity comes from a culture that treats strength as survival and obedience as virtue. Taylor-Joy’s filmography leaves little doubt that she could make that conditioning visible in every moment Lae’zel is on-screen.

Anya Taylor-Joy's performance as Beth Harmon in The Queen’s Gambit in particular reveals that she can bring a convincing blend of near-unshakable pride even in the face of profound isolation. Lae’zel’s confidence in her abilities is compelling in BG3 because it survives encounters that dismantle her understanding of the world, and Taylor-Joy would have no issue ensuring this stays intact in a live-action performance. Her penchant for precise delivery would also suit the accidental comedy of Lae’zel’s blunt observations, keeping the humor rooted in the warrior’s absolute conviction that everyone around her is being ridiculous when she finds herself at odds with the room.

When voiced by Jennifer English in BG3, Shadowheart could make even an admission of ignorance or failure feel like somebody else’s embarrassing mistake. The half-elf cleric needs an actress who can deliver that same sarcasm while also making it clear that keeping those around her at a distance takes effort. Her damaged memories and religious conditioning mean that certainty about her place in the world has to be actively maintained. Fallout, Yellowjackets, and Sweetpea star Ella Purnell could ensure the contradictions that define Shadowheart survive the transition to live-action in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series.

Viewers should want to understand Shadowheart even when she’s doing something atrocious, a quality Ella Purnell’s performance as Rhiannon in Sweetpea hinges on. Her portrayal of Lucy MacLean in Prime Video’s Fallout series shows how effectively she can capture someone discovering that the beliefs shaping her life conceal horrifying truths, another essential Shadowheart trait. Finally, her work as Jackie Taylor in Yellowjackets reveals a capacity to capture wounded pride and defensive cruelty. Together, these roles suggest that there are few actresses out there more suited to playing Shadowheart in live-action.

Regé-Jean Page already has experience in projects based on D&D. Not only that, he’s already played a character who exists in the same world as the city of Baldur’s Gate, the Forgotten Realms. As Xenk Yendar in 2023’s Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, Page brought effortless authority and wonderfully straight-faced humor to a hero whose defining personality trait is an unwavering commitment to doing good. Wyll would benefit from that same lack of embarrassment about heroism. While his character is far from simple, Wyll’s most immediate trait is that he sincerely wants to protect people.

Playing Xenk is all the proof needed that Page could make his borderline-theatrical confidence appealing while ensuring his willingness to put himself in danger feels sincere rather than sanctimonious. However, Wyll’s story also offers considerably more internal conflict than Xenk Yendar’s. His pact with the dark entity Mizora directly contradicts his noble intentions. Thankfully, Regé-Jean Page’s Simon Basset in Bridgerton showcased an ability to play polished charm that acts as a mask for concealed vulnerability and self-doubt. That experience would suit Wyll’s complicated relationship with his father and the personal costs of his pact with Mizora.

Few actors have a knack for playing approachable yet believable leadership figures like Anson Mount. His Captain Christopher Pike in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds can command a crisis and then make his colleagues feel comfortable around a dinner table. This is an excellent foundation for playing Halsin in HBO’s Baldur’s Gate series. The archdruid’s imposing appearance comes with an unusually gentle temperament. His experience gives him authority, but he rarely needs to flex his superiority. Mount could bring that reassuring confidence to a BG3 character who feels equally believable offering guidance, expressing desire, or becoming terrifying when someone threatens the vulnerable.

Any actor playing Halsin also needs to create a sense that the Baldur’s Gate character has interests beyond whatever emergency currently occupies the party. His devotion to nature, openness about pleasure, and concern for people damaged by conflict make him earthy and approachable despite his age. Anson Mount’s relaxed warmth would help those qualities emerge naturally, while his more rugged work in Hell on Wheels prove he has the action credentials for the druid’s less peaceful moments. With Halsin, the attraction is partly that strength and safety belong together, and Mount could definitely deliver this.

Long before the adventure in Baldur’s Gate 3 begins, Jaheira had already accumulated enough victories and losses to distrust a promising adventure. The veteran half-elf druid and Harper leader needs a cast member in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series who can bring that world weariness to life without turning every exchange into a solemn lesson. Hollywood veteran Michelle Pfeiffer could inarguably bring that authority, and her skills with dry humor would be just as valuable.

Pfeiffer’s Catwoman in Batman Returns is a perfect demonstration of how she can combine sharp wit with emotional baggage without making one quality cancel out the other. Her work as Lamia in 2007’s Stardust also shows how entertaining she can be in a high-fantasy setting. Jaheira needs a more grounded performance than many other Baldur’s Gate characters, with her sharpness honed by years of experience. Pfeiffer could make a cutting observation feel affectionate or devastating depending on who deserves it, while giving the character’s rarer admissions of grief the emotional weight they need.

Put physical powerhouse Dave Bautista beside a tiny hamster and much of Minsc’s visual appeal is already accounted for. The more important qualification is his understanding of how to make an enormous warrior funny through complete sincerity. As Drax in the Guardians of the Galaxy movies, Bautista repeatedly made literal-minded pronouncements entertaining because the character believed them so completely. Minsc needs that same commitment. His conversations with Boo, his miniature giant space hamster companion, should sound perfectly reasonable to him, however bewildered everyone around him becomes.

The BG3 ranger’s uncomplicated commitment to fighting evil would also give Bautista something substantial beneath the comedy. Just like Drax, Minsc’s understanding of a situation may be eccentric, but his love for his friends and determination to protect them are never minor details. Bautista has shown how tenderness can sit within an intimidating physical performance, and he could make those loyalties the reason audiences invest in the character. His size would sell the action immediately; his ability to express hurt or delight with disarming openness could ensure that Minsc remains lovable between the battles, too.

A quiet threat can be considerably more unnerving than a shouted one, and Rebecca Ferguson’s filmography proves she understands that distinction. Her Lady Jessica in Dune and Dune: Part Two combines controlled authority with a willingness to manipulate events toward ruthless ends. Those qualities would translate beautifully to Minthara, a drow paladin whose noble upbringing and brutal education inform nearly every judgment she makes. Ferguson could convey that instinctive expectation of obedience through her voice and stillness, making Minthara formidable before she ever reaches for a weapon.

However, alongside being terrifying, Minthara is also unexpectedly funny. Her devastating observations aren’t meant to be entertaining, but they often account for some of the funniest dialogue in Baldur’s Gate 3. Ferguson’s restrained delivery would suit these moments perfectly. The biggest challenge in the live-action Baldur’s Gate series would be showing the vulnerability beneath. Fortunately, thanks to roles like Juliette in Silo and Anna in The Girl on the Train, there’s every reason to believe that Rebecca Ferguson could do the subtleties of Minthara just as much justice, allowing moments of intimacy to complicate her character without erasing her more immediate, and troubling, qualities.

#3361. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The newly announced honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’

Additionally, IndieWire has announced that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

IndieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date.

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

Though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off new screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

#3360. 10 Years Later, ‘Two and a Half Men’ Star Officially Returns to CBS

Jon Cryer has continued to pop up all around television in the eleven-plus years since his Emmy-winning run on Two and a Half Men came to an end. The former Brat Pack peer enjoyed appearances in everything from NCIS to Robot Chicken, though his most extensive post-Alan Harper role was as the Arrowverse's Lex Luthor in Supergirl. NBC also briefly brought him back into the sitcom game with the short-lived Extended Family alongside Scrubs veteran Donald Faison. Yet, the one thing he hasn't done in nearly a decade is return to the home of his defining megahit comedy.

That's about to change thanks to Robert and Michelle King. Per Deadline, Cryer has been tapped for a guest appearance in the Good Wife and Elsbeth duo's new legal thriller series, Cupertino. It'll mark his first role on a CBS show since 2017, when he joined Joel McHale for an episode of his short-lived sitcom The Great Indoors. An exact date has yet to be set for when he'll meet the lawyers of Price, Siffre & Associates, but images have been revealed that tease his turn as the head of a very curious court. "Jon Cryer was perfect, playing a judge you couldn’t tell was a good guy or a bad guy," the Kings shared in an official statement. "We needed someone who could deliver the comedy but also dig into the moral dilemma of a judge who needs to follow the law in a deeply flawed system.”

Cryer's character is Judge Van Linkerspleen, who is described as a high-profile judge working behind-the-scenes in a top-secret court. As the Kings teased, he's a complex figure caught in a crooked system that values compliance above all else, though he strives to deliver rulings fairly and serve as an individual thinker within his cases. Not only will Michael Price (Mike Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) be in his presence, but so will Michael's ex, Nichole (Renée Elise Goldsberry), who appears in one of the images in what could be a tease for another legal showdown with her former flame. Cryer will join a cast that also features Ella Stiller, Nik Dodani, Busy Philipps, and Rob McClure, among others.

Reuniting the Kings with their Evil co-star, Colter, Cupertino has followed former tech start-up lawyer Michael Price and fellow canned attorney Olivia Siffre to fight back against the tech titans of Silicon Valley on behalf of everyone they've cheated. So far, they've been winning, too. From the case of a mother convinced a company's AI companion pushed her son to patricide to a legendary rapper suing an AI music studio ripping off his sound, the fledgling firm has made a name for itself as the series has become one of the most popular newcomers of the season. With only a few more episodes until CBS' primetime slate goes on break, though, the show is about to get a bit of a shakeup. Cupertino will begin airing on Sunday nights at 10 p.m. starting on January 17, as Matlock returns for Season 3 on Thursdays. After a successful trial run on the weekend earlier this month, though, it may be the perfect home for the legal thriller.

For now, Cupertino airs on Thursdays at 10 p.m. ET/PT on CBS. Get a look at Cryer in his new guest-starring role above and stay tuned here at Collider for more on his upcoming episode.

#3358. DC Finally Reveals True Face And Backstory Of Batman's Huge New Villain

DC reveals the identity of Batman's new villain, a dark mirror to Bruce Wayne with even more wealth. Batman pulls off the impossible feat of maintaining his status as a Gotham billionaire socialite while operating nightly as the Dark Knight. By day, Bruce plays the charming if slightly reckless playboy philanthropist, hosting charity galas and staging harmless public distractions that convince Gotham’s media and criminal underworld he's far too pampered and scatterbrained to ever be Batman. Behind closed doors, his strict time management and trusted allies keep Wayne Enterprises running smoothly while Bruce puts on the Batsuit to fight crime.

Gotham City’s upper crust overflows with equally wealthy and influential elites who use their fortunes for less honorable purposes. Oswald Cobblepot runs a huge financial and criminal empire from the Iceberg Lounge, Roman Sionis inherited Janus Cosmetics before building a ruthless mob syndicate, and Thomas Elliot twisted his privileged upbringing into a bitter vendetta against Bruce Wayne himself. Elsewhere in Gotham’s high society, the Court of Owls manipulates the city’s economy from opulent hidden parlors, while Ferris Boyle exploits his monopoly at the expense of innocent lives.

Batman's rogues' gallery hasn't stopped growing, and that includes rival millionaires who weaponize their wealth and influence to oppose Bruce Wayne's heroic efforts.

One full year since his introduction, DC pulls back the curtain on the mysterious mastermind who has restructured Gotham’s underworld since Batman #1. Beneath the minimalist robotic bull mask and dapper three-piece suit, the Minotaur is actually a man named "Max," whose unmasked face and true name are revealed as Batman 2026 Annual #1 takes readers straight to the center of the Torus conspiracy. Max openly declares that his real superpower is cash. He weaponizes capital and banking control to bend the city's deadliest criminals to his will.

The Minotaur's unapologetically wealth-centered philosophy sets him apart from theatrical Gotham villains, who are more commonly associated with tragic accidents, scientific experiments, or gimmicky crime enterprises. Most importantly, it frames Max as a dark mirror to Bruce Wayne himself. Without superhuman abilities, Max treats organized crime like a business as he maps out plans to take a cut of every legitimate and illicit revenue stream in Gotham within twenty months. Alongside Jesse Lonergan’s companion backup, which reveals the Calculator is secretly manipulating Max's "algorithm of crime" for his own ends, Batman 2026 Annual #1 cements the Minotaur as a grounded threat with a bottomless bankroll that rivals Batman's own.

Very few Batman villains have achieved lasting household-name status alongside icons like the Joker, Two-Face, or the Riddler in the past two decades. Professor Pyg earned genuine cult acclaim through Grant Morrison’s Batman and Robin and later video game and television appearances, and The Batman Who Laughs became ubiquitous largely through an aggressive push from DC Comics across multiple multiverse crossovers. Meanwhile, modern Gotham creations like the Designer, Failsafe, Ghost-Maker, and Punchline have struggled to maintain permanent relevance once their original arcs and writers moved on.

Absolute Batman has some of the most disturbing and terrifying villains in all of DC Comics, and they all come with something that makes them unique.

The Bronze Age of the 1970s delivered Ra’s al Ghul, Talia al Ghul, and Man-Bat in rapid succession, and the early 1990s explosion of Bane, Harley Quinn, and Victor Zsasz prove it's possible for Batman to get villains that last. For the Minotaur to avoid fading into obscurity after Matt Fraction's Torus saga wraps up, future writers will need to lean into what makes him genuinely different from traditional costumed criminals. Max's ruthless "cash as a superpower" philosophy and his role as a white-collar crime lord who can bankroll or bankrupt Gotham's classic underworld are his best assets, but he may also need to showcase a wider variety of attributes to stay around longer.

Batman 2026 Annual #1 is now available from DC Comics

#3357. Every Book in Brandon Sanderson's 'The Stormlight Archive' Series, Ranked

The Stormlight Archive is an ongoing series by Brandon Sanderson, which exists in his shared literary universe known as the Cosmere. The premise of the Cosmere is that each series or stand-alone story takes place on its own planet within the same galaxy. Each planet has a complex magic system, though some stories take place on worlds that are completely non-magical. Over the years, The Stormlight Archive has proven to be one of the flagship entries in the universe, as well as the absolute longest in terms of word count.

Currently, the saga consists of five mainline novels, two novellas, and one stand-alone double feature that consists of two short stories, though the plan is to have 10 mainline novels. Each book is over 1,000 pages long, so it can be quite time-consuming to read, but it's totally worth it. Set on the barren, windswept world of Roshar, each book features flashback sequences from particular characters, which build on their history and establish why and how they first got to use their magic. While every entry is brilliant on its own, they definitely have a hierarchy when compared against each other.

Rhythm of War is the fourth mainline novel of the series, and it's also arguably the worst. It gets off to a strong start, with a huge, climactic evacuation in an emotionally significant location, but it all kind of winds down from there. The flashbacks are a bit awkward and disjointed, split between Listener sisters Eshonai and Venli rather than just one character. Almost all of the main story is set in the city of Urithiru, with little opportunity for exploring the vastness of Roshar. The interludes don't allow for this either, as they generally focus on already-existing characters rather than following the pattern of featuring brief viewpoints of one-offs in distant lands.

By far the worst part of the story is how it just feels like one prolonged science lesson. So much of it is about how light works, how it is used in fabrials, how it can be manipulated, and the various properties of gemstones. It goes on and on and is incredibly overwhelming. Having a complex magic system isn't a problem, but the book tends to overload it a bit too much. Rhythm of War is not a bad book — in fact, it's a very good book — but it doesn't really hold up compared to the others.

Dawnshard is the second novella, which takes place between books three and four. Released alongside Rhythm of War, it is a thrilling tale across the sea to the lost island of Aimia. The main character is Rysn Ftori, a Thaylen merchant who, until then, was strictly an interlude character. Now in the leading role, Rysn desperately seeks Aimia in order to heal her pet larkin, Chiri-Chiri, who originated from the island.

However, Aimia is obstructed by a permanent storm, so this will be no easy feat. Aided by comic relief characters Lopen and his cousin, Huio, this is a simple, linear adventure to the farthest reaches of Roshar, where the mysteries of Aimia are finally unravelled after three full novels of buildup. It's not a perfect book, especially since it's only a side story, but it's a fantastic adventure with a thrilling climax that only thickens the overarching narrative.

Edgedancer is the first novella in the series, set between books two and three. The book opens with a prologue sequence that is a direct copy-and-paste of Lift's interlude from book two. This novella then continues the story, providing an exclusive look into the events that occurred afterwards. Lift takes the lead as she travels to the city of Yeddaw in Tashikk, where she hopes to try all 10 types of ceremonial pancakes made in the city. That might sound silly, but you must understand that Lift is kind of a chaos gremlin, so it's best to just go along with it.

Accompanied by Wyndle, her exhausted spren, Lift finds herself pursued by a vengeful Herald, the very same one she encountered in her interlude. The young rapscallion raises Hell in Yeddaw, ruining grain carts, befuddling guards, befriending orphans, and, as always, stealing food. It's a great, straightforward adventure into a fascinating location, with a hilarious buddy dynamic between Lift and her spren.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Wind and Truth is the fifth book in the series, and the concluding novel of the first arc. Since it marks the halfway point of the series overall, it's best not to expect a happy ending with this one. This book wasn't received quite so well by fans, mainly because it took a lot of departures from the Stormlight formula. Namely, it doesn't feature five distinct parts — instead, it features ten shorter parts, which correspond to one day. This means part one is day one, part two is day two, and so forth.

Wind and Truth is also the longest novel in the series, coming in at a whopping 1,300+ pages. The ending is tragic but fitting, and presents a beacon of hope while also spreading a blanket of darkness over the world. The flashbacks focus on the Assassin in White, Szeth-son-son-Vallano, and his time in Shinovar, which is an utterly fascinating backstory. Though many fans felt this book had a lot of shortcomings, it is absolutely action-packed, full of great character moments, and serves as a satisfying ending and new beginning all at once.

King Lopen the First of Alethkar / Elsecaller is a specially released double feature consisting of two short stories occurring concurrently, around the end of the second novel. They don't really add anything important to the overall narrative, but they do answer some burning questions that fans had. King Lopen the First of Alethkar occurs when Lopen is temporarily made king by the real king, Elhokar, as a means of creating a decoy so Elhokar can stay in hiding. Lopen is a comic relief character who, armed with a sock puppet, goes on numerous ridiculous misadventures. It's honestly the best story of the two, because it's genuinely hilarious.

Elsecaller follows what happens to Jasnah Kholin, who is missing in action for most of the book. This story isn't particularly funny; it's just Jasnah's adventure across the parallel dimension of Shadesmar as she seeks to find a way back to the Physical Realm. However, she does meet some interesting people who come from planets not yet revealed, which adds to the mystery of the Cosmere. This book might not add much to the story, but it is incredibly fun and quick to read.

The Way of Kings is the very first book in the series, which is nothing short of mind-blowing. It's where readers are first introduced to the world of Roshar, along with its strangeness, size, and variety. The flashbacks centre on Kaladin, a soldier-turned-slave, who is used as arrow fodder in the war between the Listeners and the Alethi. Meanwhile, Dalinar Kholin, uncle of Alethkar's king, begins experiencing strange visions and becomes convinced he needs to unite the 10 Alethi highprinces in their efforts to defeat their enemies, rather than constantly maneuvering against each other in court.

In the distant city of Kharbranth, a young student named Shallan Davar hopes to study with Jasnah Kholin, Elhokar's sister and Dalinar's niece, and one of the brightest scholars in Roshar. This might be the shortest mainline novel in the series (though it is still roughly 1,000 pages long), but it is an absolute masterpiece, not only in its worldbuilding, but in its inspirational moments and action-packed climax. The Way of Kings is one of Sanderson's finest works and is still recommended as an entry point to the Cosmere by many fans.

Words of Radiance is the second mainline novel in the series, picking up immediately where The Way of Kings leaves off. Instead of featuring Kaladin's flashbacks, the book sets its sights on Shallan Davar's past and her childhood growing up in rural Jah Keved. Words of Radiance is commonly cited as the absolute best of the series, with a lot of fans deeming it their favorite, and it's really not hard to see why.

The climax is absolutely unbelievable, genuinely filling the reader with anxiety, dread, sorrow, joy, and relief all at once. There are so many quotable moments in this book, from the fight scene in the arena to Szeth's first encounter with a Herald. A lot changes, yet a lot stays the same, all while the stakes are raised higher than ever before. This book is a solid 10 out of 10. It doesn't waste a single word, and is consistently exciting, even when little is happening.

Oathbringer takes the crown as being the absolute best of the entire saga (so far, anyway). The flashbacks are about Dalinar Kholin and his life as a terrifying combatant. Since much of Dalinar's history is marked by constant civil war and political upheavals, most of his flashbacks are chock-full of violence, with a few major and minor battles scattered in between. Outside of the flashbacks, the story is brilliant, too.

There are numerous large-scale battles that take place throughout the narrative, including the Siege of Kholinar and the climactic Battle of Thaylen Field. There are even more quotable moments in this book, and some utterly devastating death scenes, too. There's so much going on in this novel, yet it's never hard to keep track of things. Oathbringer is honestly one of the greatest fantasy novels ever written, and that's really saying something.
